meta.title: Food Poisoning
meta.description: Comprehensive information on food poisoning, including causes, symptoms, complications, diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and public health aspects. Based on IFFGD patient guide and EMRC.

meta.disclaimer: For education and chatbot assistance only. Not a substitute for medical diagnosis or treatment.

epidemiology.seasonality: Increased during summer and rainy seasons

transmission_cycles.short_cycle: Person-to-person via contaminated food and food handlers

pathogenesis.entry: Ingestion of contaminated food or water
pathogenesis.intestinal_phase: Invasion of Peyer’s patches in terminal ileum
pathogenesis.gallbladder_colonization: Source of relapse and chronic carriage

hematology: Normal or low total leukocyte count

carrier_state.definition: Excretion of Salmonella Typhi for ≥12 months

principles: Do not delay treatment awaiting culture results

meta.disclaimer: For education and chatbot assistance only. Not a substitute for medical diagnosis or treatment.

transmission_cycles.long_cycle: Environmental contamination of food and water

pathogenesis.entry: Ingestion of contaminated food or water
pathogenesis.systemic_phase: Absorption of toxins or spread of infection

public_health_significance: Can spread infection through food handling

diagnosis.clinical_challenge: Symptoms overlap with other gastrointestinal illnesses

overview.definition: Food poisoning, also called foodborne illness, is an infection or irritation of the digestive tract that spreads through food or drinks. Viruses, bacteria, and parasites cause most cases. Harmful chemicals may also cause food poisoning.
overview.typical_course: Most often acute (sudden onset, short duration). Most cases last less than a week and resolve without treatment. In some cases, it can last longer or lead to serious complications.
overview.prevalence_in_us: About 48 million people in the United States have food poisoning each year. It causes about 3,000 deaths annually in the US.

risk_groups.note: Food safety is especially important for these groups.

dehydration.description: Most common complication. Loss of fluids and electrolytes due to vomiting and diarrhea. Without replacement, the body cannot work properly.
dehydration.danger_groups: Especially dangerous in children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.
dehydration.consequences_if_untreated: Organ damage, shock, coma, or death.

hemolytic_uremic_syndrome_HUS.description: A kidney condition where red blood cells are destroyed and block the kidneys' filtering system, leading to acute kidney injury (sudden, temporary loss of kidney function).
hemolytic_uremic_syndrome_HUS.common_cause: Infection with E. coli O157:H7 (other bacteria/viruses can also cause it).

other_complications: Health problems during pregnancy and pregnancy complications (e.g., Listeria can cause miscarriage or stillbirth).
Guillain-Barré syndrome (most commonly after Campylobacter jejuni infection).
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) after various bacteria, viruses, or parasites.
Breathing problems due to botulism (Clostridium botulinum) and some fish/shellfish poisoning affecting nervous system and paralyzing breathing muscles.
Reactive arthritis (after Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella, and others).

symptoms.duration: Range from mild to severe, last from a few hours to several days.
symptoms.note_nervous_system: If nervous system symptoms occur, see a doctor or go to an emergency room right away.

in_adults: Light-headedness, dizziness (especially upon standing), or fainting
Decreased skin turgor (pinched skin does not flatten back right away)
in_infants_and_young_children: Urinating less than usual, or no wet diapers for 3 hours or more
symptoms_of_dehydration.action: Anyone with signs of dehydration should see a doctor or go to an emergency room right away.

for_adults: Change in mental state (irritability, lack of energy, confusion)
Six or more loose stools in a single day
Diarrhea that continues for more than 3 days
Severe pain in abdomen or rectum
Stools that are black and tarry or contain blood/pus
Symptoms of dehydration or other complications
Unable to drink enough liquids or oral rehydration solutions
No improvement after drinking oral rehydration solutions
for_infants_and_children: Change in mental state (irritability, lack of energy)
Diarrhea lasting more than a day
Any fever in infants; high fever in older children
Severe pain in abdomen or rectum
Infant, premature birth, or other medical conditions
Unable to drink enough liquids or oral rehydration solutions
No improvement after oral rehydration solutions
seek_immediate_care.note: Diarrhea is especially dangerous in newborns and infants – can lead to severe dehydration in a day or two. Untreated dehydration can cause death within a day.

microbes.description: Infections with viruses, bacteria, and parasites cause most food poisoning. Microbes can spread at any point: growth, harvest, slaughter, processing, storage, shipping, preparation.
foods_that_may_contain_microbes: Raw or undercooked meat, poultry, eggs
Unpasteurized dairy products and fruit juices
Deli foods (sliced meat, salads, cut fruit, sandwiches, baked goods)
Processed and ready-to-eat meats (hot dogs, deli meat)
microbes.cross_contamination: If raw foods are not kept separate, microbes can spread to other foods, hands, utensils, cutting boards, and surfaces.
microbes.growth_conditions: Microbes grow if food not cooked thoroughly, cooked food not kept hot, or perishable food not promptly refrigerated/frozen.
microbes.person_to_food_spread: Infected people can spread microbes to food if they don't wash hands thoroughly after using bathroom, changing diapers, and before preparing food.

bacteria: Certain Clostridium (C. perfringens, C. botulinum – causes botulism)
chemicals: Fish and shellfish containing toxins from algae or bacteria
Unwashed produce with large amounts of chemical pesticides
causes.travelers_diarrhea: Caused by contaminated food or water with bacteria, parasites, or viruses when traveling from US to developing countries. Usually acute, but some parasites cause longer diarrhea.

diagnosis.typical_approach: Doctors often diagnose based on symptoms – mild/short-lasting cases usually do not need tests.
physical_exam: Check blood pressure and pulse for dehydration
Check for fever or dehydration signs
Tap abdomen for tenderness or pain
Digital rectal exam to check for blood in stool (indicates bacteria or parasites)
diagnosis.stool_tests: Can show presence of viruses, bacteria, or parasites.
diagnosis.blood_tests: Can show signs of infections or complications like dehydration.

treatment.self_care: Most people get better without medical treatment. Replace lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration. Over-the-counter medicines may help in some cases.

replacement_fluids_and_electrolytes.for_adults_with_severe_diarrhea_or_risk: Older adults, immunocompromised, severe diarrhea, or dehydration symptoms should drink oral rehydration solutions (Pedialyte, Naturalyte, Infalyte, Ceralyte).
replacement_fluids_and_electrolytes.for_children: Give oral rehydration solution as directed – talk to doctor for infants. Infants should continue breast milk or formula as usual.

over_the_counter_medicines.warnings: Can be dangerous for infants and children – talk to doctor before giving. Do NOT use if you have bloody diarrhea or fever (signs of bacterial/parasitic infection) – see a doctor instead.

medical_treatment.bacteria_or_parasites: Doctors may prescribe antibiotics or antiparasitic medicines, plus rehydration solutions.
medical_treatment.probiotics: May help shorten diarrhea, but talk with doctor before using – especially for children, older adults, or immunocompromised.
medical_treatment.hospitalization: For severe dehydration, hemolytic uremic syndrome, paralysis, or other life-threatening symptoms.

safe_handling_practices: Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs separate from other foods
Prepare salads and refrigerate them before handling raw animal products
Promptly refrigerate or freeze perishable foods
Wash hands with soap and water before and after handling food
Wash fruits and vegetables before eating, cutting, or cooking
Cook foods long enough and at high enough temperatures to kill harmful microbes
Wash utensils and surfaces after each use
Do not eat perishable foods left out for >2 hours (or >1 hour if temperature >90°F)
prevention.food_recalls: Watch for food recalls. If a food is recalled because it may cause illness, check if you have it – do not eat it; return to store or dispose.

avoid: Unbottled/unfiltered tap, well, lake, or river water (also for brushing teeth)
Ice, foods, drinks made with untreated water
Raw or undercooked meat, fish, shellfish
travelers_diarrhea_prevention.pre_travel_advice: Talk with doctor before traveling. May recommend ways to treat local water, bring antibiotics (e.g., rifaximin, rifamycin, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin). Some immunocompromised individuals may take antibiotics before and during trip to prevent travelers' diarrhea.

diet_and_nutrition.what_to_eat: Drink plenty of liquids to replace fluids and electrolytes. When appetite returns, most people can go back to normal diet even if diarrhea persists. For children, give usual foods as soon as appetite returns. Infants should have breast milk or formula as usual.
what_to_avoid: Caffeinated drinks (coffee, tea, some soft drinks)
High-fat foods (fried foods, pizza, fast foods)
Foods/drinks with large amounts of simple sugars (sweetened beverages, some fruit juices)
Milk and milk products (lactose) – some people have trouble digesting lactose for up to a month after food poisoning
diet_and_nutrition.restricted_diet_note: Research shows following a restricted diet does not help treat diarrhea. Most experts do not recommend fasting or restricted diet when you have diarrhea.

clinical_trials.description: Research studies on food poisoning, including treatments for norovirus infection, vaccines for E. coli, prevention of travelers' diarrhea.
clinical_trials.note: Always talk with your healthcare provider before participating in a clinical study.

faq.question: What is food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning, also called foodborne illness, is an infection or irritation of your digestive tract that spreads through food or drinks. Viruses, bacteria, and parasites cause most food poisoning. Harmful chemicals may also cause it. It is most often acute (sudden and short-lasting). Most cases last less than a week and people get better on their own without treatment.

faq.question: How common is food poisoning in the US?
faq.answer: Each year, about 48 million people in the United States have food poisoning. It causes about 3,000 deaths in the US each year.

faq.question: Who is more likely to get food poisoning?
faq.answer: Anyone can get food poisoning, but infants and children, pregnant women and their fetuses, older adults, and people with weak immune systems are more likely to get it. These groups are also more likely to have severe symptoms or complications.

faq.question: What are the common symptoms of food poisoning?
faq.answer: Common symptoms include diarrhea or bloody diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, and headache. Symptoms range from mild to severe and may last from a few hours to several days. Less commonly, some types (like botulism or fish/shellfish poisoning) can affect the nervous system, causing blurred vision, headache, paralysis, tingling/numbness, or weakness.

faq.question: What are the signs of dehydration from food poisoning?
faq.answer: In adults: extreme thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual, light-headedness/dizziness/fainting, tiredness, dark urine, decreased skin turgor (pinched skin doesn't flatten quickly), sunken eyes or cheeks. In infants/children: thirst, dry mouth, less urination or no wet diaper for 3+ hours, lack of energy, no tears when crying, decreased skin turgor, sunken eyes or cheeks.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor for food poisoning?
faq.answer: Adults should see a doctor right away if they have: change in mental state (irritability, confusion, lack of energy), high fever, frequent vomiting, six or more loose stools in a day, diarrhea lasting >3 days, nervous system symptoms, severe abdominal or rectal pain, black/tarry or bloody/pus stools, signs of dehydration, inability to drink enough fluids, or no improvement after oral rehydration solutions. Also older adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised should seek care. For infants and children, don't hesitate – call a doctor for any symptoms, especially diarrhea lasting >1 day, any fever in infants, or any sign of dehydration.

faq.question: What causes food poisoning?
faq.answer: Most food poisoning is caused by infections with viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A), bacteria (Salmonella, Clostridium, Campylobacter, Staph, E. coli, Vibrio, Listeria), or parasites (Toxoplasma, Giardia, Cryptosporidium). Harmful chemicals in certain fish/shellfish, wild mushrooms, or unwashed produce with pesticides can also cause it. Microbes can spread during growing, harvesting, processing, storage, shipping, or preparation.

faq.question: How is food poisoning treated at home?
faq.answer: The most important treatment is replacing lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration. Drink plenty of water, diluted fruit juices, sports drinks, broths, and eat saltine crackers. For severe diarrhea or high-risk individuals, use oral rehydration solutions like Pedialyte, Naturalyte, Infalyte, or Ceralyte. Over-the-counter medicines like loperamide (Imodium) or bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) may help adults, but do not use if you have bloody diarrhea or fever – see a doctor instead. Never give these to children without a doctor's advice.

faq.question: When do doctors prescribe antibiotics for food poisoning?
faq.answer: Doctors may prescribe antibiotics or antiparasitic medicines if the food poisoning is caused by bacteria or parasites. They are not effective against viruses. For travelers' diarrhea, antibiotics like rifaximin, rifamycin, azithromycin, or ciprofloxacin may be prescribed. Always consult a doctor – do not self-treat with antibiotics.

faq.question: What are the serious complications of food poisoning?
faq.answer: Dehydration is the most common complication. Others include hemolytic uremic syndrome (kidney failure, most often from E. coli O157:H7 in young children), Guillain-Barré syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, breathing problems from botulism or shellfish poisoning, reactive arthritis, and pregnancy complications (including miscarriage or stillbirth from Listeria).

faq.question: How can I prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs separate from other foods; promptly refrigerate perishables; wash hands with soap before and after handling food; wash fruits and vegetables; cook foods thoroughly at high enough temperatures; wash utensils and surfaces after each use; don't leave perishable food out for more than 2 hours (1 hour if >90°F). Watch for food recalls. For travelers to developing countries, avoid tap water, ice from untreated water, unpasteurized dairy, street vendor food, raw/undercooked meat/seafood, and unwashed/unpeeled produce.

faq.question: What should I eat when recovering from food poisoning?
faq.answer: Drink plenty of liquids to replace fluids and electrolytes. When your appetite returns, you can usually go back to your normal diet even if diarrhea continues. For children, give their usual foods as soon as appetite returns. Infants should continue breast milk or formula. Avoid caffeine, high-fat foods, foods with lots of simple sugars (sweetened drinks, some juices), and milk products (lactose) for up to a month, as they may make symptoms worse.

Always seek the advice of your healthcare provider with any questions regarding a medical condition. The International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders (IFFGD) does not endorse any specific products or treatments mentioned.

microbiological_criteria_fsanz.document_title: Compendium of Microbiological Criteria for Food
microbiological_criteria_fsanz.author: Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ)

introduction.purpose: Provide best practice guidance for food regulators and the food industry, including basic information on microorganisms significant to food safety and microbiological criteria for food safety management.
introduction.through_chain_management: Microbiological safety is best ensured by implementing hygiene controls at each stage of the food chain. Microbiological testing supports through-chain control measures.

microbiological_criteria_types.food_safety_criteria: End-point criteria to determine safety of a food lot. Regulatory requirements in Standard 1.6.1 and Schedule 27 of the Food Standards Code.
microbiological_criteria_types.process_hygiene_criteria_PHC: Applied to verify hygiene measures or process controls are working as intended. Based on indicator organisms, applied at specified points in manufacturing.
microbiological_criteria_types.guideline_criteria: Used to check that food for sale is safe and suitable, and that food handling controls are adequate. Indicate whether microbiological status is within normal/acceptable range.

introduction.proactive_management: Applying PHC at various stages helps detect loss of control before food safety limit is exceeded. Useful for identifying contamination sources in complex processes.

glossary.aseptic_technique: Method of collecting sample to prevent contamination during sampling.
glossary.commercial_laboratory: Should hold NATA accreditation (Australia) or equivalent.
glossary.composite_sample: Consolidation of multiple samples from same lot for qualitative testing only. Max 15x25g composited → result 'absent in 375g'.
glossary.corrective_actions: Actions to bring process back under control and prevent recurrence.
glossary.lot_batch: Amount of food prepared under essentially same conditions, usually within 24 hours.
glossary.microbiological_guideline_criteria: Criteria to verify overall food handling controls and hygienic practices.
glossary.pre_requisite_programs: Essential food safety practices documented in manufacturer's food safety program.
glossary.process_hygiene_criteria: Criteria to verify hygiene or process control at a specified point.
glossary.qualitative_tests: Establish presence/absence (e.g., L. monocytogenes not detected in 25g).
glossary.quantitative_tests: Determine number of organisms per gram or ml (e.g., 150 E. coli/g).
glossary.representative_samples: Sample that reflects properties of entire batch.
glossary.root_cause_analysis: Investigation to identify cause of failure.
glossary.sample_integrity: Ensuring no contamination during sampling; aseptic collection, temperature-controlled transport.

sampling_plans.2_class_plan: Used for pathogens not permitted. n = sample units, c = max allowable positive units, m = limit (e.g., n=5, c=0, m=not detected).
sampling_plans.3_class_plan: Used for quantitative tests. m = good/marginal limit, M = unacceptable limit, c = max number of samples allowed between m and M.

glossary.testing_method: Should be most recent Australian Standard (AS 5013) or ISO or validated equivalent.

abbreviations.CPS: Staphylococcus aureus and other coagulase-positive staphylococci

ready_to_eat_foods.definition: Foods intended to be consumed without any further process that would eliminate or reduce pathogenic microorganisms.
ready_to_eat_foods.purpose_and_scope: Provide guideline microbiological criteria for assessment of RTE foods, including limits and follow-up actions. Not for lot acceptance/rejection but for evaluating food handling controls.
microbiological_tests_choice_factors: Whether ingredients are cooked or raw
Whether food requires temperature control for safety (pH, water activity)

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Cooked rice dishes (sushi), potato/pasta dishes, meat/vegetable/fish stews and curries.
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Spores widespread, survive cooking, activated by heat. Slow cooling or warm storage allows growth and toxin production.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Undercooked/improperly handled poultry, raw meat, unpasteurised milk, contaminated water.
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Colonise intestines of food-producing animals. Cross-contamination to RTE foods from raw meat/poultry.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Vacuum-packed foods (sous vide), home-canned/bottled foods, fermented/salted/smoked meat/seafood, honey (infant botulism).
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Spores survive cooking, germinate in anaerobic conditions, produce toxin even at low temperatures.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Cooked meats (rolled joints, large pieces), meat-containing products (stews, gravies, curries, pies), vegetable dishes.
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Spores survive cooking, slow cooling/reheating of large volumes provides warm anaerobic conditions for growth.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Soft cheeses, delicatessen meats, cooked chicken, smoked seafood, salads, rockmelon – especially those with extended refrigerated shelf life that support growth.
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Widespread in environment, persists in processing environments. Post-process contamination from contact surfaces. Grows at refrigeration temperatures.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Eggs (raw/lightly cooked), poultry, raw meat, milk/dairy, fresh produce (leafy greens, sprouts, melons), low moisture foods (spices, peanut butter, chocolate, flour).
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Reservoir in intestinal tracts of vertebrates. Cross-contamination, poor hygiene, temperature abuse.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Inadequately cooked ground beef, uncooked fermented comminuted meat (salami), raw/unpasteurised dairy, fresh produce (leafy greens, sprouted seeds).
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Ruminants (cattle, sheep) are major reservoir. Faecal contamination of environment, water, or direct.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: High-protein foods requiring extensive handling: meat, poultry, eggs, milk/dairy, cream/custard bakery products, sandwich fillings.
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Food handlers main source (nasal passages, throat, skin). Contamination via hands/respiratory secretions. Time/temperature abuse allows growth and enterotoxin production.

bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.associated_foods: Fish, shellfish, crustaceans (particularly raw molluscs and crustacea).
bacterial_pathogen_food_associations.why: Natural contaminant of seafood from coastal/estuarine waters. Growth under inadequate refrigeration.

interpretation_categories.satisfactory: Within expected levels, no food safety concern. No action required.
interpretation_categories.marginal: Upper range of expected levels. Some action may be required to ensure controls remain effective.
interpretation_categories.unsatisfactory: Outside expected levels, indicates poor practices. Further actions to re-establish controls.
interpretation_categories.potentially_hazardous: Exceeds levels that present immediate food safety concern. Prevent distribution/sale, determine source, implement corrective actions.

Bacillus_cereus.potentially_hazardous: > 10⁵ cfu/g – inadequate time/temperature control during cooling/storage, poor quality raw ingredients, inadequate acidification. Actions: product disposition, investigate cooling/storage profiles, review raw ingredient limits.
Bacillus_cereus.unsatisfactory: 10³ – ≤10⁵ – same causes. Actions: investigate cooling/storage, review raw ingredients.
Bacillus_cereus.marginal: 10² – <10³ – process controls not fully achieved or raw material contamination. Proactive investigation.

Campylobacter_spp.potentially_hazardous: Detected in 25g – inadequate processing (poultry, raw milk) or cross-contamination, untreated water. Actions: product disposition, assess cooking/pasteurisation, cross-contamination prevention, water treatment.
Campylobacter_spp.satisfactory: Not detected in 25g (note: freezing reduces levels, avoid frozen samples)

Clostridium_perfringens.potentially_hazardous: >10⁵ – inadequate time/temperature control during cooling/storage/reheating, slow cooling of large volumes. Actions: product disposition (toxin cannot be destroyed), review temperature/time profiles, assess production volume capacity.
Clostridium_perfringens.unsatisfactory: 10³ – ≤10⁵ – same as above. Investigate cooking/cooling/reheating profiles.
Clostridium_perfringens.marginal: 10² – <10³ – process controls not fully achieved. Proactive investigation.

Listeria_monocytogenes_growth_can_occur.potentially_hazardous: Detected in 25g – post-processing contamination or inadequate process control. Actions: product disposition (consider vulnerable consumers), investigate raw materials, cleaning/sanitising, premises construction, process flow, shelf life, temperature control.

Listeria_monocytogenes_growth_will_not_o.potentially_hazardous: >10² – post-processing contamination or inadequate control. Product disposition.
Listeria_monocytogenes_growth_will_not_o.satisfactory_if_listericidal_process_not: Detected but ≤10² – indicates better process control needed. Investigate if listericidal process was applied; trend analysis.

Salmonella_spp.potentially_hazardous: Detected in 25g – inadequate processing, cross-contamination, contaminated raw materials, poor time/temperature control. Actions: product disposition, investigate raw materials, processing adequacy (cooking, pH, water activity), cross-contamination prevention, cleaning/sanitising, time/temperature controls, possible infected food handler.

Enterobacteriaceae_including_coliforms.unsatisfactory: >10⁴ cfu/g – post-process contamination, inadequate processing, poor time/temperature. Actions: review processing controls, cleaning/sanitising, food handler hygiene, time/temperature control.
Enterobacteriaceae_including_coliforms.marginal: 10² – 10⁴ – some cross-contamination or inadequate processing. Proactive investigation.

Escherichia_coli.unsatisfactory: >10² – faecal contamination from poor hygiene (cross-contamination, inadequate processing, primary production environment). Actions: review processing controls, cleaning/sanitising, handler hygiene, time/temperature, primary production controls (harvest, water, fertilisers).
Escherichia_coli.marginal: 3 – <10² – low levels may occasionally occur, but widespread detection suggests poor hygiene. Proactive investigation.

Listeria_spp_other_than_monocytogenes.unsatisfactory: >10² – conditions favourable for L. monocytogenes, poor controls or cross-contamination, poor temperature control or shelf life. Actions: investigate raw materials, cleaning/sanitising, premises construction, process controls. Consider environmental sampling and specific L. monocytogenes testing.
Listeria_spp_other_than_monocytogenes.marginal: ≤10² – controls may become problematic. Proactive investigation.

standard_plate_count_categories.Category_1: Foods fully cooked for immediate sale/consumption (hot takeaway pizza, fish & chips). Satisfactory <10³, Marginal 10³–<10⁵, Unsatisfactory ≥10⁵.
standard_plate_count_categories.Category_2a: All components cooked, minimal handling/storage (whole pies, sausage rolls, quiches, whole cooked chicken). Satisfactory <10⁴, Marginal 10⁴–<10⁶, Unsatisfactory ≥10⁶.
standard_plate_count_categories.Category_2b: All components cooked, minimal handling, packaged for extended refrigerated shelf life (cook/chill meals, vacuum-packed sliced meats). Satisfactory <10⁴, Marginal 10⁴–<10⁷, Unsatisfactory ≥10⁷.
standard_plate_count_categories.Category_3: All components cooked, some handling/refrigerated storage before sale (chilled/portioned pies, unpackaged sliced meats, cooked shellfish). Satisfactory <10⁵, Marginal 10⁵–<10⁷, Unsatisfactory ≥10⁷.
standard_plate_count_categories.Category_4: Contains some uncooked components (dips hummus/tzatziki, bakery with fresh cream/uncooked fillings, sandwiches, sushi). Satisfactory <10⁶, Marginal 10⁶–<10⁷, Unsatisfactory ≥10⁷.
standard_plate_count_categories.Category_5: Inherently high plate count due to normal flora or processing (fermented foods: cured meats, sauerkraut, yoghurt, cheese; preserved: pickled; dried: fruits, nuts, spices; fresh produce). No limits – N/A.

process_control_table.pre_operational_environment: Control pathogen presence via cleaning/sanitation, dry conditions. Monitoring records, environmental monitoring.
process_control_table.pasteurisation: Control via time/temperature. Verified pasteurisation records. In-process samples meet PHC: SPC n=5 c=2 m=500/g M=5000/g AND Enterobacteriaceae n=10 c=2 m=0/10g.
process_control_table.evaporation_spray_drying: Control post-pasteurisation contamination via PRPs. Same PHC as pasteurisation.
process_control_table.dry_blending: Control via PRPs, raw material control. Same PHC.
process_control_table.packing_final_product: Control via PRPs. Product meets microbiological guideline criteria.

powdered_infant_formula.microbiological_guideline_criteria_abbre: For Cronobacter (Enterobacter sakazakii) and Salmonella: n=30, c=0, not detected in 10×10g each for Cronobacter and Salmonella. For indicator organisms: Enterobacteriaceae n=10 c=0 m=0/10g; SPC target values provided.
powdered_infant_formula.corrective_actions: Failure to meet criteria indicates trend toward loss of control. Actions: evaluate product safety through increased final product testing for Cronobacter and Salmonella before release; evaluate environmental and process hygiene controls before production resumption.

meat_products_raw_chicken.process_hygiene_criteria_Campylobacter: Target <10,000 cfu per whole chicken carcass at end of processing (after final chill, before dispatch). Recommended lower limit of detection methods available (down to 100 cfu/carcass). Corrective actions: review process controls including feed withdrawal, evisceration, decontamination, chilling.
meat_products_raw_chicken.Salmonella: No numerical target but serotypes should be identified. S. Typhimurium or S. Enteritidis must be notified to relevant authority. Controls similar to Campylobacter.
verification_points: Live bird receipt: feed withdrawal 8-12 hours, no unacceptable carcasses.
Evisceration: inspection, removal of unacceptable carcasses.
Carcase decontamination: wash with >5 ppm free available chlorine, pH 5-7, ORP >650mV.
Storage/distribution: chill to <7°C within 6 hours of stunning, ≤5°C within 12 hours.
meat_products_raw_chicken.method_of_analysis: AS 5013.6, or modified method using 200ml rinse and plating onto 8+1 plates, LOD 100 cfu/carcass.

dairy_products.introduction: Main hazards: Salmonella, L. monocytogenes, S. aureus, B. cereus, pathogenic E. coli, Cronobacter. Control through primary production, transport, processing. Microbiological testing verifies controls.
dairy_products.testing_process: Representative aseptic samples, 2-class or 3-class plans. Composite samples allowed for qualitative tests. Quantitative tests individual. NATA-accredited lab. Corrective actions and root cause analysis for failures.

sampling_plans_and_frequency.alternative_for_small_batches: Single sample (n=1, c=0, result must not exceed m).
sampling_plans_and_frequency.frequency_based_on_risk: Every 10 or 20 batches; for extended periods, at least once every 2 months.

indicator_organisms.coliforms: Historically common, heat-processed foods high coliform indicates under-processing or post-process contamination.
indicator_organisms.Enterobacteriaceae: Better indicator for heat-treated foods; all killed by pasteurisation, so presence indicates inadequate processing or post-process contamination.
indicator_organisms.Escherichia coli: Specific indicator of faecal contamination. Presence indicates recent contamination.
indicator_organisms.standard_plate_count: General quality indicator; interpretation depends on processing and shelf life.

pathogens.Listeria_monocytogenes: Common in moist processing environments; environmental monitoring key.
pathogens.Salmonella_spp: Survives long in dry environments, can colonise equipment.
pathogens.Staphylococcus_aureus_CPS: On skin of handlers, tolerant to low water activity (aw 0.83).

product_categories.criteria: SPC <50,000 cfu/ml (premium <20,000); Bulk Milk Cell Count <400,000 cells/ml. Regulatory requirement under Standard 4.2.4.

product_categories.tests: CPS: n=5 c=1 m=100 M=1000; E. coli OR Coliforms OR Enterobacteriaceae: n=5 c=2 m=3 M=10 / m=10 M=100 / m=10 M=100; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g; Frequency: every 20 batches. For unsalted: every 10 batches. For products with post-pasteurisation inclusions: every 10 batches.

product_categories.tests_all_cheese: CPS: n=5 c=2 m=100 M=1000; E. coli: n=5 c=1 m=10 M=100; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g (if supports growth) every 20 batches.
product_categories.soft_semi_soft_cheese_>39%_moisture_pH>5: CPS: n=5 c=0 m=100; E. coli: n=5 c=1 m=10 M=100; Salmonella: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g; frequency every 10 batches.
product_categories.cheese_with_post_pasteurisation_inclusio: L. monocytogenes, CPS, E. coli every 10 batches.
product_categories.shredded_grated_cut_cheese: Salmonella, L. monocytogenes, CPS, E. coli every 10 batches.

product_categories.raw_milk_cheese_criteria: CPS: n=5 c=2 m=100 M=1000; Staphylococcal enterotoxins: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g; E. coli: n=5 c=1 m=10 M=100; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g; Salmonella: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g. Frequency: every batch until consistently met as advised by regulator.

product_categories.pH>4.5: CPS: n=5 c=2 m=100 M=1000; E. coli/Coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae: n=5 c=1 m=3 M=10 / m=10 M=100 / m=10 M=100; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g; frequency every 10 batches.
product_categories.pH<4.5: Testing reduced frequency; Salmonella every 10 batches, CPS/E. coli every 20 batches, L. monocytogenes n=5 c=0 m=100 every 20 batches.
product_categories.pH<4.5_with_high_risk_inclusions: CPS, E. coli/coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae, L. monocytogenes, Salmonella every 10 batches.

product_categories.process_control: Enterobacteriaceae or coliforms in-process: n=5 c=0 m=10/g (or m=10/g M=100/g). Finished product: Salmonella n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g every 20 batches; B. cereus n=5 c=1 m=100 M=1000 every 20 batches.

product_categories.tests: E. coli/coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae: n=5 c=1 m=3 M=10 etc; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 m=100; CPS: n=5 c=2 m=100 M=1000; Salmonella: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g for products with high-risk ingredients. Frequency: every 20 batches (yoghurt), every 10 batches for higher risk.

product_categories.product: Ice cream and other frozen products
product_categories.frozen_ice_cream: E. coli/coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae: n=5 c=1 m=3 M=10 etc; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 m=100; Frequency every 20 batches. For products with high-risk inclusions, also test Salmonella every 20 batches.
product_categories.refrigerated_soft_serve_mix: E. coli/coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae every 10 batches; L. monocytogenes n=5 c=0 not detected in 25g every 10 batches.

product_categories.milk: E. coli/coliforms/Enterobacteriaceae: n=5 c=1 m=3 M=10 etc; L. monocytogenes: n=5 c=0 not detected in 25ml; frequency every 10 batches.

failure_microbiological_guideline_criter: Immediate: isolate affected product, notify regulator, determine if production stop needed.

Investigative: review records, test raw materials, in-process and related batches, disassemble equipment, enhanced environmental sampling (Zones A-D), enhanced cleaning/disinfection, root cause analysis.
Follow-up: product disposition (recall/withdrawal), initiate clearance program, document incident.
corrective_actions.failure_process_hygiene_criteria: Review the specific process step being verified, test finished product against guideline criteria to assess impact.

dairy_products.clearance_program: After a pathogen detection, test 30 samples from first batch after re-start, then day 3 (30 samples), day 5 (30 samples), day 12 (30 samples). All must meet guidelines. Product held until negative results confirmed.
dairy_products.environmental_monitoring: See Chapter 6. Includes zones A (product contact), B (non-product contact close), C (further away), D (outside processing area).

environmental_monitoring.introduction: Preventing food contamination from processing environment is critical. Environmental monitoring more effective than end-product testing for identifying contamination sources.

zones.Zone_A: Product contact surfaces – conveyors, tables, benches, vats, utensils, pumps, valves, slicers, mixers, packing/filling machines, seals/gaskets.
zones.Zone_B: Non-product contact surfaces in close proximity to product or flow – conveyors exterior, equipment control panels, service lines, equipment above exposed product, keypads, door handles.
zones.Zone_C: Non-product contact surfaces further away – drains, walls, floors, mats, condensate, hoses, trolleys, pallets, conveyor belts, overhead piping, forklifts, refrigeration units.
zones.Zone_D: Outside processing area – locker rooms, cafeterias, entry ways, loading bays.

corrective_actions_by_zone.Zone_A: Hold potentially affected product, increase sampling, review access restrictions and staff hygiene, review cleaning and sanitising, review sanitary design of equipment, clean and sanitise, resample until three consecutive negatives, test associated product (day of, before, after positive).
corrective_actions_by_zone.Zone_B: Increase sampling, review access restrictions, review Zone C results, reassess cleaning and sanitising, clean and disinfect, resample to verify efficacy.

Listeria_monocytogenes_monitoring.frequency: Higher for RTE foods that support growth.
Listeria_monocytogenes_monitoring.corrective_actions: If Zone A positive for Listeria spp., test for L. monocytogenes, hold product pending result. If L. monocytogenes confirmed in Zone A or B, prevent product release, fix problem, monitor effectiveness.

pathogens_detailed.name: Bacillus cereus
pathogens_detailed.description: Spore-forming, widespread in environment. Two syndromes: emetic (pre-formed toxin, rapid onset 1-5h) and diarrhoeal (toxin produced in intestine, onset 8-16h). Illness generally >10⁵ cfu/g.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Emetic: rice dishes, starchy foods. Diarrhoeal: meat, vegetable, fish dishes with spices.
pathogens_detailed.control: Cool cooked foods rapidly to ≤5°C or hold ≥60°C. Acidification to pH <4.6 controls growth. Minimum water activity 0.93.

pathogens_detailed.name: Campylobacter spp.
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-negative, microaerophilic. C. jejuni and C. coli main species. Infective dose as low as 100 cells. Incubation 2-5 days, illness 2-10 days. Symptoms: fever, diarrhoea (bloody), abdominal cramps. Can lead to reactive arthritis or Guillain-Barré syndrome.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Raw poultry, raw milk, contaminated water.
pathogens_detailed.control: Avoid cross-contamination, cook poultry thoroughly, pasteurise milk, use potable water. Cannot grow in foods but survive refrigeration. Easily killed by cooking.

pathogens_detailed.name: Clostridium botulinum
pathogens_detailed.description: Spore-forming anaerobe produces potent neurotoxin. Types A, B, E, F cause human illness. Symptoms start 18-36h: vertigo, nausea, double vision, muscle weakness, paralysis, respiratory failure. Infant botulism from spores in honey.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Vacuum-packed foods, sous vide, home-canned/bottled foods, fermented/salted/smoked meat/seafood, honey.
pathogens_detailed.control: Maintain strict hygiene and temperature protocols, control pH (Group I pH ≤4.6, Group II pH ≤5.0 inhibits growth), discard bulging or spoiled preserved foods. Do not feed honey to infants <12 months.

pathogens_detailed.name: Clostridium perfringens
pathogens_detailed.description: Anaerobic spore-former. Illness from ingestion of >10⁶ vegetative cells, enterotoxin causes profuse diarrhoea and cramps ~16h after consumption. Fast doubling time <10 min.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Cooked meats (beef, poultry) and meat-containing products (gravies, stews, curries), large volumes cooled too slowly.
pathogens_detailed.control: Cool cooked food from 60°C to 21°C within 2 hours, then to 5°C within further 4 hours. Reheat to >70°C rapidly. Minimum pH 5.5, water activity 0.97.

pathogens_detailed.name: Listeria monocytogenes
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-positive, grows at refrigeration temperatures (<5°C). Causes listeriosis: non-invasive (mild) or invasive (fatality 20-30%). At-risk: pregnant women (miscarriage, stillbirth), elderly, immunocompromised. High numbers typically needed.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Soft cheeses, deli meats, cooked chicken, pre-prepared salads, pâté, smoked seafood, rockmelon. Extended refrigerated shelf life and post-process contamination key.
pathogens_detailed.control: Minimise raw material contamination, use listericidal processes (cooking/pasteurisation), prevent post-process contamination, restrict growth via shelf life, cold chain, or formulation. Growth not supported if pH<4.4 or aw<0.92 or combination pH<5.0 and aw<0.94.

pathogens_detailed.name: Salmonella spp. (non-typhoidal)
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-negative, over 2500 serotypes. S. Typhimurium most common in Australia. Infective dose low. Symptoms 12-36h: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps, fever, duration 4-7 days.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Eggs (raw eggs), poultry, raw meat, milk/dairy, fresh produce (leafy greens, sprouts, melons), low moisture foods (spices, peanut butter, chocolate, flour).
pathogens_detailed.control: Prevent cross-contamination, apply lethal processing step, maintain temperature control. Minimum growth temperature ~7°C, pH as low as 3.8 under some conditions, minimum water activity 0.93.

pathogens_detailed.name: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC)
pathogens_detailed.description: Produce Shiga toxins. O157:H7 most common globally; in Australia also O111, O26, O113. Infective dose 10-100 cells. Symptoms: bloody diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, vomiting. Can cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), kidney failure. Children under 5 and elderly most susceptible.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Undercooked ground beef, uncooked fermented comminuted meat (salami), raw/unpasteurised dairy, fresh produce (leafy greens, sprouted seeds).
pathogens_detailed.control: Prevent faecal contamination at primary production, adequate cooking (core 75°C), pasteurisation, fermentation controls (pH, water activity). Minimum growth pH 4.4, water activity 0.95.

pathogens_detailed.name: Shigella spp.
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-negative, non-motile. Humans only natural host. Highly infectious (10-200 cells). Symptoms 8-50h: watery diarrhoea, cramps, nausea, fever; severe cases dysentery (blood/mucus). Can lead to reactive arthritis or HUS.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Foods handled extensively and consumed raw (salads, sandwiches).
pathogens_detailed.control: Stringent personal hygiene, ill handlers must not handle food, proper cooking/pasteurisation, separate raw/RTE, clean and sanitise, use potable water. Grows 6-47°C, tolerant to low pH, salt 4-5%.

pathogens_detailed.name: Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase-positive staphylococci)
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-positive, produces heat-stable enterotoxins. Found on skin and mucous membranes of humans (50% carriers). Toxin produced when S. aureus grows to 10⁵-10⁸ cfu/g. Onset 1-7h: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea. Recovery within 2 days.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Handled foods: cream/custard bakery, sandwich fillings, meat/poultry/egg products, salads (potato, tuna, chicken).
pathogens_detailed.control: Minimise time at 5-60°C (2-hour/4-hour rule). Good hygiene: use gloves/tongs, handwashing, avoid sneezing/coughing over food. Cooking kills cells but not toxin. Grows at aw as low as 0.83, pH 4.0-10.0.

pathogens_detailed.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
pathogens_detailed.description: Gram-negative curve-shaped rod, salt-tolerant, natural in coastal and estuarine waters. Pathogenic strains cause gastroenteritis with diarrhoea (bloody), abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. Infective dose >10⁵ cells. Onset 4h to a few days.
pathogens_detailed.associated_foods: Fish, shellfish, crustaceans (raw molluscs, cooked crustacea).
pathogens_detailed.control: Chill seafood quickly to <5°C after harvest, maintain refrigeration. Cooking to internal temperature 65°C destroys organism. Prevent cross-contamination. Grows at 5-43°C (optimum 37°C), generation time 9-10 min.

indicator_microorganisms_detailed.name: Coliforms
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.description: Group of Enterobacteriaceae that ferment lactose rapidly (24-48h) producing acid and gas. Not a well-defined taxonomic group.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.purpose: Historically common indicator, especially in dairy sector for post-pasteurisation hygiene. High counts in heat-processed foods indicate under-processing or post-process contamination.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.interpretation: Presence does not necessarily indicate faecal contamination (coliforms are normal flora of raw foods). High levels warn of unhygienic handling or ineffective processing.

indicator_microorganisms_detailed.name: Enterobacteriaceae
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.description: Family of Gram-negative, non-spore forming bacteria including pathogens (Salmonella, pathogenic E. coli, Shigella, Cronobacter) and non-pathogens.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.purpose: Useful to assess adequacy of processing and hygiene practices for heat-treated foods. All killed by pasteurisation/cooking, so presence indicates inadequate processing or post-process contamination.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.interpretation: Expected high levels in raw plant foods. Psychrotrophic members can grow in chilled foods, making interpretation over shelf life difficult. Best used on day of production.

indicator_microorganisms_detailed.name: Escherichia coli
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.description: Gram-negative, facultative anaerobic rod, normal intestinal flora of warm-blooded animals. More specific indicator of faecal contamination than coliforms or Enterobacteriaceae.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.purpose: Indicator of faecal contamination and hygiene effectiveness. For raw commodities: GMP/GHP of slaughter, GAP for produce, harvest water quality. For heat-treated foods: post-process contamination or inadequate processing.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.interpretation: Best indicator of recent faecal contamination. Can become established in factory environments. Absence does not guarantee absence of enteric pathogens.

indicator_microorganisms_detailed.name: Listeria spp.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.description: Genus including L. monocytogenes (human pathogen) and non-pathogenic species (L. innocua, L. ivanovii, etc.). Gram-positive, grows at refrigeration temperatures, widespread in environment, forms biofilms.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.purpose: Testing for Listeria spp. indicates whether conditions favour L. monocytogenes growth/survival. Broader indicator increases chance of detecting harbourage sites.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.interpretation: In RTE foods: presence indicates inadequate processing or cross-contamination. Higher levels (>100 cfu/g) suggest poor temperature control or overextended shelf life. In environment: positive result should trigger corrective actions (cleaning, sanitising, increased monitoring).

indicator_microorganisms_detailed.name: Standard Plate Count (SPC)
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.description: Total number of aerobic mesophilic microorganisms that form colonies under specified conditions (typically 30°C).
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.purpose: Indicates microbiological quality, not safety. Useful for trend analysis over time.
indicator_microorganisms_detailed.interpretation: Depends heavily on product and processing. Raw commodities: 10⁶-10⁷ cfu/g normal. Fermented foods: high counts from starter cultures. Heat-processed foods: should be <10³-10⁴ cfu/g right after processing. Shelf life increases counts (unless growth prevented).

metadata.title: Foodborne Pathogens: Hazards, risk analysis and control
metadata.publisher: Woodhead Publishing Ltd and CRC Press LLC
metadata.description: Comprehensive reference on foodborne pathogens, covering risk assessment, detection methods, control strategies, and detailed profiles of bacterial, viral, parasitic, and fungal hazards.

chapter_1_introduction.trends: Foodborne disease increasing globally; in UK cases rose from under 10,000 in 1977 to >90,000 in 1998. Salmonellosis decreased in US/UK due to vaccination; campylobacteriosis continues to rise.
chapter_1_introduction.incidence_US: Estimated 76 million illnesses, 325,000 hospitalizations, 5,000 deaths annually; known pathogens cause 14 million illnesses.
chapter_1_introduction.surveillance: Systems include laboratory reporting, physician reports, outbreak investigations. Underreporting estimated 20-100x for salmonellosis.
chapter_1_introduction.emerging_pathogens: EHEC (E. coli O157:H7), Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella Typhimurium DT104, Listeria monocytogenes, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora.
chapter_1_introduction.factors: Demographics (aging, immunocompromised), consumer trends (fresh foods, eating out), global sourcing, intensive agriculture.

chapter_2_detecting_pathogens.conventional_methods: Plate count, MPN, enrichment, selective/differential media.

rapid_methods.electrical: Impedance/conductance (Malthus, Rabit, Bactometer). Detection time correlates with microbial load.
rapid_methods.ATP_bioluminescence: Measures ATP from living cells; rapid hygiene testing (surfaces, equipment).
rapid_methods.microscopy: DEFT (direct epifluorescent filter technique), flow cytometry, solid phase cytometry.
rapid_methods.immunological: ELISA, latex agglutination, immunochromatography (dipstick). Specific antibodies.
rapid_methods.nucleic_acid: DNA probes, PCR (BAX, Probelia, TaqMan), NASBA. High sensitivity, can detect non-culturable cells.
rapid_methods.immunomagnetic_separation: Concentration of target pathogens from food.

chapter_2_detecting_pathogens.quality_control_vs_quality_assurance: QC relies on testing; QA uses HACCP with testing for verification, validation, troubleshooting.

chapter_3_modelling.types: Kinetic growth models, growth boundary models, death models, survival models.
chapter_3_modelling.growth_parameters: Lag phase, growth rate, maximum population density.
chapter_3_modelling.applications: Product/process design, shelf-life prediction, HACCP, risk assessment.

chapter_4_risk_assessment.definition: Risk = f(probability, severity). Hazard = agent with potential to cause harm.
chapter_4_risk_assessment.steps: Hazard identification, exposure assessment, hazard characterization (dose-response), risk characterization.
chapter_4_risk_assessment.tools: Stochastic (Monte Carlo) simulation, sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis.
chapter_4_risk_assessment.food_safety_objectives: ICMSF proposal linking risk assessment to HACCP and performance criteria.

chapter_5_HACCP_farm.principles: 7 principles, 12 steps. Critical Control Points (CCPs) on farms: animal purchase, feeding, housing, medication, manure management.
chapter_5_HACCP_farm.challenges: Pathogens cannot be eliminated; detection difficult; good husbandry practices essential.
chapter_5_HACCP_farm.examples: Beef cattle HACCP plan (breeding, parturition, grazing, housing, parasite control). Dairy milking hygiene, mastitis control.

chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.levels: Factory site (pest control, landscaping), building (walls, floors, drainage), internal barriers (high-risk vs low-risk areas).
chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.personnel_hygiene: Changing rooms, handwashing, footwear, protective clothing.
chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.air_handling: Positive pressure, HEPA filtration, 5-25 air changes per hour, temperature 10-12°C for chilled foods.
chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.floors: Resin screeds or vitrified ceramic tiles, coved, waterproof, cleanable.
chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.drainage: Channel drains, fall 1:50 to 1:100, separate drains for high/low risk.
chapter_6_hygienic_plant_design.sanitation: Cleaning (mechanical, chemical, thermal, time) and disinfection (chlorine, QACs, amphoterics, alcohols). ATP bioluminescence for monitoring.

chapter_7_safe_process_design.principles: Identify target pathogens, raw material quality, process lethality, prevent recontamination.
chapter_7_safe_process_design.heat_treatments: Pasteurization (70°C/2min), sterilization (121°C/3min for low-acid canned foods).
chapter_7_safe_process_design.equipment: Hygienic design (smooth, self-draining, no dead spaces), easy cleanability.

chapter_8_HACCP_implementation.prerequisites: GMP, cleaning, pest control, supplier QA, training.
chapter_8_HACCP_implementation.hazard_analysis: Distinguish safety from quality; focus on significant hazards.
chapter_8_HACCP_implementation.documentation: Simple records for CCPs (monitoring, corrective actions).
chapter_8_HACCP_implementation.maintenance: Verification audits, training refreshers, trend analysis.

chapter_9_food_handlers_consumers.home_as_risk: Major location for foodborne outbreaks; consumer education critical.
chapter_9_food_handlers_consumers.risk_factors: Inadequate storage, cross-contamination, undercooking, infected handlers.
chapter_9_food_handlers_consumers.training: Needs to address knowledge, attitudes, practices; use of behavioral models (Theory of Planned Behavior, Health Belief Model).
chapter_9_food_handlers_consumers.social_marketing: Apply marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion) to change consumer behaviors.

chapter_10_pathogenic_E_coli.overview: Includes EPEC, ETEC, EIEC, EHEC (VTEC/STEC). VTEC O157:H7 major concern; low infectious dose (<100 cells).
chapter_10_pathogenic_E_coli.symptoms: Haemorrhagic colitis (bloody diarrhea), HUS (kidney failure, especially in children).
chapter_10_pathogenic_E_coli.associated_foods: Undercooked ground beef, raw milk, fresh produce (lettuce, sprouts), unpasteurized apple juice, fermented sausages.
chapter_10_pathogenic_E_coli.detection: Selective enrichment (mTSB+novobiocin), immunomagnetic separation, CT-SMAC agar, latex agglutination, PCR (BAX, TaqMan).
chapter_10_pathogenic_E_coli.control: Raw material control (farm hygiene, manure management, slaughter hygiene); thermal process (70°C/2min); fermentation (pH drop, drying); washing (chlorine 200 ppm); segregation raw/cooked.

chapter_11_Salmonella.overview: >2400 serotypes; S. Enteritidis and S. Typhimurium most common. Infective dose typically >10^5 but can be low (<100) in high-fat foods.
chapter_11_Salmonella.symptoms: Gastroenteritis (diarrhea, fever, cramps) 12-36h; enteric fever (S. Typhi); septicemia.
chapter_11_Salmonella.associated_foods: Eggs, poultry, meat, milk, chocolate, peanut butter, fresh produce (sprouts, melons).
chapter_11_Salmonella.detection: Pre-enrichment (buffered peptone water), selective enrichment (Rappaport-Vassiliadis, selenite-cystine), selective agars (XLD, Hektoen, BGA), PCR, ELISA.
chapter_11_Salmonella.control: Pasteurization of milk/eggs; cooking 70°C/2min; good agricultural practices; biosecurity; carcass decontamination (steam, organic acids); prevent cross-contamination.

chapter_12_Listeria_monocytogenes.overview: Psychrotrophic, grows at refrigeration temperatures. High mortality (20-30%) in at-risk groups (pregnant, elderly, immunocompromised).
chapter_12_Listeria_monocytogenes.symptoms: Meningitis, septicemia, miscarriage, stillbirth; also febrile gastroenteritis with high doses.
chapter_12_Listeria_monocytogenes.associated_foods: Soft cheeses, deli meats, smoked seafood, pâté, prepared salads, rockmelon.
chapter_12_Listeria_monocytogenes.detection: Enrichment (Fraser broth), selective agars (Oxford, Palcam), PCR, ELISA, immunochromatography.
chapter_12_Listeria_monocytogenes.control: Heat treatment (70°C/2min); prevent post-process contamination; environmental monitoring (zones A-D); effective cleaning/sanitation; shelf-life limits; consumer advice for at-risk groups.

chapter_13_Campylobacter_Arcobacter.Campylobacter: C. jejuni leading bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in developed countries. Low infectious dose (hundreds of cells). Symptoms: diarrhea (bloody), abdominal pain, fever; can lead to Guillain-Barré syndrome.
chapter_13_Campylobacter_Arcobacter.associated_foods: Raw/undercooked poultry, raw milk, contaminated water.
chapter_13_Campylobacter_Arcobacter.detection: Selective enrichment (Bolton, Preston broths), microaerophilic incubation, CCDA agar, PCR.
chapter_13_Campylobacter_Arcobacter.control: Farm biosecurity, disinfection of drinking water, rapid slaughter processing, carcass decontamination, thorough cooking, prevent cross-contamination.
chapter_13_Campylobacter_Arcobacter.Arcobacter: A. butzleri, A. cryaerophilus. Associated with pork, poultry, water. Detection: CAT agar, PCR. Control: proper cooking, chlorination.

chapter_14_other_bacteria.Staphylococcus_aureus: Enterotoxin pre-formed in food; symptoms rapid-onset vomiting. Control: refrigeration (<10°C prevents toxin), hygiene, avoid temperature abuse.
chapter_14_other_bacteria.Shigella: Low infectious dose (10-100 cells). Human reservoir. Symptoms: bloody diarrhea (dysentery). Control: handwashing, avoid infected handlers, proper cooking.
chapter_14_other_bacteria.Yersinia_enterocolitica: Psychrotrophic, grows at 4°C. Associated with pork. Symptoms: enterocolitis, may mimic appendicitis. Control: cooking, prevent cross-contamination.
chapter_14_other_bacteria.Vibrio: V. parahaemolyticus, V. vulnificus, V. cholerae. Associated with seafood (raw oysters). Control: refrigeration, cooking, avoid raw shellfish for high-risk individuals.
chapter_14_other_bacteria.Aeromonas: Opportunistic; associated with seafood, water. Control: disinfection of water, thorough cooking.
chapter_14_other_bacteria.Plesiomonas: Associated with oysters, water. Control: similar to Vibrio.

chapter_15_spore_formers.Clostridium_botulinum: Produces potent neurotoxin. Types A, B, E, F. Spores heat-resistant. Control: 12-D process (121°C/3min), pH <4.6, aw <0.94 (NaCl 10%), refrigeration <3.3°C for non-proteolytic strains.
chapter_15_spore_formers.Clostridium_perfringens: Produces enterotoxin in gut. Rapid growth (doubling 8-10 min). Control: rapid cooling (60°C to 21°C in 2h, then to 5°C in 4h), reheat to >70°C.
chapter_15_spore_formers.Bacillus_cereus: Emetic toxin (cereulide) pre-formed in starchy foods; diarrheal toxin produced in gut. Control: rapid cooling, refrigeration, avoid prolonged holding at ambient temperatures.

chapter_16_viruses.important: Norwalk-like caliciviruses (NLV), hepatitis A virus (HAV), rotavirus, astrovirus, enteric adenovirus.
chapter_16_viruses.characteristics: Small, non-enveloped, resistant to heat, pH, disinfectants. Cannot grow in food.
chapter_16_viruses.symptoms: NLV: vomiting, diarrhea (onset 24-48h). HAV: hepatitis (incubation up to 50 days).
chapter_16_viruses.associated_foods: Shellfish, fresh produce (berries, salads), contaminated water, foods handled by infected persons.
chapter_16_viruses.detection: RT-PCR, ELISA (for rotavirus, adenovirus). No culture for NLV.
chapter_16_viruses.control: Hand hygiene, exclusion of sick food handlers, proper sanitation (1000 ppm chlorine), depuration of shellfish, HAV vaccination.

chapter_17_parasites.Cryptosporidium_parvum: Oocysts resistant to chlorine, infective dose 10-100. Symptoms: watery diarrhea; chronic in immunocompromised. Control: filtration of water, pasteurization, avoid raw produce from contaminated areas.
chapter_17_parasites.Giardia_duodenalis: Cysts resistant. Symptoms: diarrhoea, malabsorption. Control: good hygiene, filtration of water, cooking.
chapter_17_parasites.Cyclospora_cayetanensis: Oocysts sporulate in environment. Symptoms: watery diarrhea, fatigue. Control: washing produce, avoid imported raspberries/basil from endemic areas.

chapter_18_toxigenic_fungi.mycotoxins: Aflatoxins (Aspergillus flavus/parasiticus), ochratoxin A (Penicillium verrucosum, Aspergillus ochraceus), patulin (Penicillium expansum), fumonisins (Fusarium moniliforme).
chapter_18_toxigenic_fungi.aflatoxins: Carcinogenic (liver). Control: drying crops, storage at low aw, sorting, ammonia treatment.
chapter_18_toxigenic_fungi.ochratoxin_A: Nephrotoxic; control: good storage, HACCP in coffee processing.

micro_organisms_and_food.summary: Foods carry microbial associations; microbes can cause spoilage, foodborne illness, or beneficial fermentation.
micro_organisms_and_food.food_spoilage_preservation: Early preservation methods relied on water activity reduction (drying, salting, sugar, smoking). Industrial revolution led to canning, chilling, freezing. Post-harvest losses in developing countries exceed 20% for perishables.
micro_organisms_and_food.food_safety: Foodborne disease is a major health problem; biological contaminants are the major cause.
micro_organisms_and_food.fermentation: Microbes can positively transform foods (e.g., fermented products).

sections.microbiological_quality_assurance: Food microbiologists assure safe, wholesome food through knowledge of microbial ecology and processing effects.

sections.diversity_of_habitat: Microbes found in extreme environments; play roles in carbon, nitrogen, sulfur cycles.
sections.atmosphere: Air is hostile; Gram-positive rods and cocci dominate; pigmented colonies; Bacillus and Streptomyces spores common. 'Open air factor' kills Gram-negatives.
sections.soil: Rich reservoir; Bacillus and Clostridium spores survive heat; soil organisms cause spoilage.
sections.water: Marine bacteria are psychrophilic and halophilic; fish spoilage; sewage contamination leads to enteric pathogens in shellfish; E. coli as indicator.
sections.plants: Phylloplane and rhizoplane flora; yeasts (Sporobolomyces, Bullera), moulds (Cladosporium, Aureobasidium), bacteria (Pectobacterium, Pseudomonas, Lactobacillus). Field fungi (Cladosporium, Alternaria) and storage fungi (Penicillium, Aspergillus).
sections.animals: Skin has specialized flora (Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium); nose and throat carry Staphylococcus aureus.

chapter_3.title: Factors Affecting the Growth and Survival of Micro-organisms in Foods

sections.microbial_growth: Exponential growth: dx/dt = μx, doubling time τ = 0.693/μ. Growth curve: lag, exponential, stationary phases. Logistic equation models carrying capacity.

intrinsic_factors.nutrient_content: Microbes derive nutrients from foods; Monod equation: μ = μmS/(S+Ks).
intrinsic_factors.pH_and_buffering: pH affects enzyme activity. Weak organic acids inhibit by penetrating membrane, acidifying cytoplasm. pKa values of common food acids given.
intrinsic_factors.redox_potential_Eh: Measured by platinum electrode; oxygen most influential. Aerobes require positive Eh, anaerobes negative. Methylene blue and resazurin tests.
intrinsic_factors.antimicrobial_barriers: Integument (skin, shell); plant antimicrobials: isothiocyanates, allicin, phytoalexins, essential oils (eugenol, thymol, cinnamic aldehyde). Animal sources: lysozyme, lactoferrin, avidin, lactoperoxidase.
intrinsic_factors.water_activity_aw: aw = P/P0 = ERH/100. Raoult's law: aw ≈ Xwater. Minimum aw for growth: Gram-negatives 0.97, Gram-positives 0.90, yeasts 0.88, moulds 0.80, halophiles 0.75, xerophiles 0.61. Halotolerant, osmotolerant, xerotolerant. Water sorption isotherms show hysteresis.

extrinsic_factors.relative_humidity: High RH can increase food aw, leading to microbial growth.
extrinsic_factors.temperature: Cardinal temperatures: thermophiles (40-45°C min, 55-75°C opt, 60-90°C max), mesophiles (5-15°C min, 30-40°C opt, 40-47°C max), psychrophiles (-5 to +5°C min, 12-15°C opt, 15-20°C max), psychrotrophs (-5 to +5°C min, 25-30°C opt, 30-35°C max). Arrhenius law not followed; membrane fluidity important.
extrinsic_factors.gaseous_atmosphere: CO2 inhibits microbial growth; effect increases with decreasing temperature. Mechanism: pH drop, membrane effects, enzyme inhibition.

sections.implicit_factors: Growth rate, affinity (Ks), stress responses (heat shock, RpoS), mutualism, antagonism, commensalism.
sections.predictive_food_microbiology: Hurdle effect; probabilistic, response surface, kinetic models. Gompertz, Baranyi equations. Square root model: √k = b(T - Tmin). ComBase Predictor, Pathogen Modeling Programme.

heat_processing.pasteurization: 60-80°C; eliminates pathogens or spoilage organisms. HTST milk 71.7°C/15s.
heat_processing.appertization: >100°C; commercial sterility. 12D botulinum cook: F0 = 12 × D121 = 2.52 min.
heat_processing.D_and_z_values: D = decimal reduction time; z = temperature change for 10× change in D. Log-linear death kinetics.
heat_processing.heat_sensitivity: Vegetative cells D65 0.02-3 min; spores D121 0.1-4 min.
heat_processing.spoilage_of_canned_foods: Flat sour (Bacillus), thermophilic spoilage, sulfur stinker, leaker spoilage.
heat_processing.aseptic_packaging: UHT processing (130-140°C, seconds) with sterile filling.

irradiation.UV: 260 nm most lethal; low penetration; D values 3-200 × 10^2 ergs.
irradiation.ionizing: Gamma rays (Co-60), electrons, X-rays. Doses: radicidation (pathogen elimination), radurization (shelf-life extension), radappertization (sterilization). 6D doses: E. coli 1.5-3 kGy, Salmonella 3-5, C. botulinum 20-30, viruses >30 kGy.

sections.high_pressure_processing: Pascalization; 400-600 MPa; inactivates vegetative cells; spores require heat combination.

low_temperature_storage.chill_storage: 0-5°C; psychrotrophs dominate; generation times: pseudomonad 6.7h at 5°C, 26.6h at 0°C.
low_temperature_storage.freezing: <-18°C; no growth; aw reduced; survival of pathogens (Salmonella up to 7 years).

chemical_preservatives.organic_acids: Benzoic (pKa 4.19), sorbic (pKa 4.8), propionic (pKa 4.9), acetic, lactic. Undissociated form active.
chemical_preservatives.nitrite: Inhibits C. botulinum; forms nitrosamines; gives cured meat colour.
chemical_preservatives.sulfur_dioxide: Active at low pH; inhibits bacteria, yeasts, moulds.

sections.modification_of_atmosphere: Vacuum packing, MAP (CO2, O2, N2), CAP. Extends shelf-life by inhibiting aerobes.
sections.control_of_water_activity: Drying, salting, sugar; intermediate moisture foods (aw 0.85-0.6).
sections.compartmentalization: Butter: water droplets in fat phase; microbial growth limited.

sections.spoilage_definition: Deprivation of good qualities; often sudden due to exponential growth. Specific spoilage organisms (SSO).

milk.microflora: Sources: udder interior (micrococci, streptococci), teat exterior, milking equipment. Psychrotrophs dominate after refrigeration. Payment based on total bacterial count.
milk.heat_treatment: LTH 62.8°C/30min, HTST 71.7°C/15s, UHT 135°C/1s. Phosphatase test. Spoilage: psychrotrophic Gram-negatives, Bacillus (bitty cream).

meat.structure_and_composition: Muscle: water 75%, protein 19%, lipid 2.5%, carbohydrate 1.2%. pH drops to 5.4-5.5; DFD (dark, firm, dry) meat pH >6.2; PSE (pale, soft, exudative) in pigs.
meat.primary_processing: Skinning, evisceration, washing; counts 10^2-10^4 cfu/cm^2. Poultry scalding (50°C), defeathering, evisceration.
meat.spoilage: Aerobic: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Psychrobacter; off-odours at 10^7 cfu/cm^2. Vacuum-pack: lactic acid bacteria.

fish.microbiology: Skin: 10^2-10^7 cfu/cm^2; Gram-negatives (Pseudomonas, Shewanella, Vibrio). Psychrotrophic. Spoilage: TMA production by Shewanella putrefaciens and Photobacterium phosphoreum.

plant_products.cereals: Field fungi (Fusarium, Alternaria, Cladosporium) require high aw; storage fungi (Penicillium, Aspergillus) grow at lower aw (0.71-0.82).
plant_products.fruits: Low pH; spoilage by fungi (Penicillium, Botrytis). Patulin in apple juice.
plant_products.vegetables: Higher pH; bacterial spoilage by Pectobacterium, Pseudomonas, Xanthomonas.

sections.food_hazards: Natural toxicants (solanine, cyanogenic glycosides, lectins, favism), microbial hazards.
sections.significance: Foodborne disease widespread; costs billions; malnutrition-diarrhoea cycle.
sections.incidence: Under-reporting; IID study England: 9.4 million cases/year; 1 in 5 people. Salmonella isolations declined post-1997; Campylobacter increased.
sections.risk_factors: Mass catering; factors: preparation too far in advance, storage at ambient temperature, inadequate cooling, cross-contamination.
sections.emerging_pathogens: Listeria monocytogenes, Campylobacter, VTEC, Enterobacter sakazakii. Factors: farming changes, international trade, processing changes, population movement, lifestyle, microbial evolution.
sections.alimentary_tract: Mouth (saliva), stomach (pH 0.8-5.0), small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), large intestine (colon). Microflora: 10^2-10^3/ml duodenum, 10^10-10^11/g faeces.
sections.pathogenesis_of_diarrhoea: Pre-formed toxin (Staph. aureus, B. cereus), non-invasive infection (cholera toxin, LT, ST, C. perfringens enterotoxin), invasive infection (Salmonella, Shigella, EIEC, EHEC).

Aeromonas_hydrophila.characteristics: Psychrotrophic; grows at 0-1°C; produces enterotoxins; associated with water, fish, meat.

Bacillus_cereus.characteristics: Spore-forming, aerobic; grows 8-55°C, min aw 0.95. Emetic toxin (cereulide) heat-stable; diarrhoeal toxin (HBL, NHE) heat-labile.
Bacillus_cereus.foods: Rice, starchy foods (emetic); meat, vegetables, sauces (diarrhoeal).

Campylobacter.characteristics: Microaerophilic, 42°C optimum; D55 2.5-6.6 min. Infective dose ~500 cells.

Clostridium_botulinum.characteristics: Anaerobic spore-former. Group I (proteolytic): min pH 4.6, min aw 0.94, D121 0.1-0.2 min; Group II (non-proteolytic): min pH 5.0, min aw 0.97, grows at 3.3°C, D80 0.6-3.3 min.
Clostridium_botulinum.foods: Canned foods, smoked fish, honey (infant botulism).

Clostridium_perfringens.characteristics: Anaerobic, spore-former, grows 12-50°C, optimum 43-47°C, generation time 7.1 min. D100 0.31->38 min. Enterotoxin produced during sporulation.
Clostridium_perfringens.control: Rapid cooling (60°C to 21°C/2h, to 5°C/4h), reheating to >70°C.

Enterobacter_sakazakii.symptoms: Meningitis, necrotising enterocolitis in infants; 50% mortality.
Enterobacter_sakazakii.control: Pasteurization (72°C/15s gives >10 log reduction); hygiene during reconstitution.

Escherichia_coli.pathotypes: EPEC, ETEC, EIEC, EHEC (VTEC/STEC), EAggEC, DAEC.
Escherichia_coli.EHEC_O157:H7: Low infective dose (<100 cells). Symptoms: haemorrhagic colitis, HUS (10% of children under 10). Foods: undercooked ground beef, raw milk, fresh produce, unpasteurized juice. Control: cooking 71.1°C internal, acidification, hygiene.

Listeria_monocytogenes.characteristics: Psychrotrophic, grows 0-42°C, min pH 4.4, min aw 0.92, salt tolerant (10% NaCl). D60 5-8.3 min, D70 seconds.
Listeria_monocytogenes.foods: Soft cheeses, deli meats, pâté, smoked fish.
Listeria_monocytogenes.control: Cooking 70°C/2min, avoid post-process contamination, environmental monitoring.

Mycobacterium_species.M._bovis: Causes bovine tuberculosis; killed by pasteurization; acid-fast.
Mycobacterium_species.M._paratuberculosis: Linked to Crohn's disease; heat resistance controversial.

sections.Plesiomonas_shigelloides: Oxidase-positive, grows 8-45°C; associated with shellfish; mild diarrhoea.

Salmonella.characteristics: >2400 serotypes; S. Enteritidis, S. Typhimurium most common. Infective dose typically 10^5-10^8 but low (<100) in fatty foods. D72 in milk: S. Senftenberg 0.09 min, S. Typhimurium 0.003 min.
Salmonella.foods: Eggs, poultry, meat, milk, chocolate, peanut butter.
Salmonella.control: Pasteurization, cooking, vaccination of poultry, hygiene.

Staphylococcus_aureus.characteristics: Grows 7-48°C, min aw 0.83, salt tolerant (20%). Enterotoxins (A-J) heat-stable.
Staphylococcus_aureus.control: Refrigeration (<10°C prevents toxin), hygiene, avoid handling.

Vibrio.V._parahaemolyticus: Associated with seafood; Kanagawa-positive strains pathogenic.

sections.Scombrotoxic_fish_poisoning: Histamine produced by bacterial decarboxylases; symptoms: flushing, headache, diarrhoea; control: rapid chilling.

helminths_and_nematodes.Trichinella_spiralis: Trichinellosis; undercooked pork; freezing (-15°C/30d) kills larvae.

protozoa.Cryptosporidium_parvum: Oocysts; raw milk, water; chlorine resistant.
protozoa.Cyclospora_cayetanensis: Raspberries, basil; outbreaks in North America.

toxigenic_fungi.aflatoxins: Aspergillus flavus/parasiticus; B1 most toxic; carcinogenic; occurs in groundnuts, maize. LD50 in humans ~1 mg/kg?; M1 in milk.
toxigenic_fungi.ochratoxin_A: Penicillium verrucosum, Aspergillus ochraceus; nephrotoxic; cereals, coffee, wine.
toxigenic_fungi.patulin: Penicillium expansum; apples, apple juice; limit 50 μg/kg.
toxigenic_fungi.fumonisins: Fusarium verticillioides; maize; associated with oesophageal cancer.

foodborne_viruses.norovirus: Small round structured viruses; projectile vomiting; shellfish, salads.

spongiform_encephalopathies.BSE: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy; linked to vCJD; prion agent.

sections.lactic_acid_bacteria: Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, Leuconostoc, Pediococcus. Homofermentative (EMP) vs heterofermentative (phosphoketolase). Bacteriocins (nisin).

fermented_milks.yoghurt: Strep. thermophilus and Lb. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus; pH 3.8-4.2; acetaldehyde flavour.
fermented_milks.buttermilk: Lactococcus lactis, Leuconostoc; diacetyl from citrate.

sections.cheese: Rennet coagulation; starter LAB; Cheddar, Camembert, Blue.

fermented_vegetables.sauerkraut: Leuconostoc mesenteroides, then Lactobacillus plantarum; 2-3% salt.
fermented_vegetables.olives: Lye treatment to remove oleuropein; Lactobacillus plantarum; salt 5-8%.

sections.fermented_meats: Salami; Lactobacillus sake, Pediococcus; nitrate reducing Micrococcaceae; pH <5.2.
sections.beer: Barley malt; Saccharomyces cerevisiae; hops; wort; fermentation (8-18°C).
sections.vinegar: Two-stage: yeast (ethanol) then Acetobacter (acetic acid). Orleans, quick vinegar, submerged acetification.

mould_fermentations.soy_sauce: Aspergillus oryzae (koji) then LAB and yeasts in brine.

chapter_10.title: Methods for the Microbiological Examination of Foods

sections.indicator_organisms: Coliforms, faecal coliforms, E. coli, Enterobacteriaceae.
sections.direct_examination: Microscopy, Breed smear, DEFT (acridine orange, viability stains).
sections.cultural_techniques: Agar media; selective, elective, resuscitation, diagnostic.
sections.enumeration_methods: Pour plate, spread plate, Miles-Misra, spiral plater, MPN, hydrophobic grid membrane filter.

alternative_methods.electrical_methods: Conductance, impedance; detection time correlated with count.

rapid_methods.DNA/RNA: Gene probes, PCR, multiplex PCR, nested PCR, RT-PCR, real-time PCR.

chapter_11.title: Controlling the Microbiological Quality of Foods

sections.quality_and_criteria: Safety, acceptability/shelf-life, consistency. Standard, specification, guideline.

sampling_schemes.two_class_attributes: n, c, m. Operating characteristic (OC) curves.
sampling_schemes.variables_acceptance: Log-normal distribution; x̄ + k1 s > V for rejection.

sections.quality_control: Ineffective without source control; MMB payment scheme effective.

control_at_source.facilities: Layout, cleaning, pest control, high/low risk separation.
control_at_source.equipment: Hygienic design principles; cleanable, self-draining, no dead spaces.
control_at_source.cleaning_and_disinfection: Two-stage: detergent cleaning then disinfection (chlorine, iodophors, QUATs, amphoterics). CIP systems.

sections.risk_analysis: Risk assessment (hazard identification, exposure assessment, hazard characterization, risk characterization), risk management, risk communication. Food safety objectives (FSO).
