chapter_1_equipment.title: Equipment
chapter_1_equipment.scope: General requirements and guidance for handling, maintenance, performance check and calibration of equipment used in food microbiology laboratory.

equipment_list.name: Biosafety Cabinet/Laminar Air Flow
equipment_list.description: Enclosed workspace with HEPA filter (99.97% of particles >0.3 μm) to protect analyst and environment. Classes I, II, III.
equipment_list.use: Protect from airborne infection; work in middle to rear; avoid gas burner; use disposable equipment.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Check working surface and walls for contamination; expose PCA plates for 30 min; no colonies.
equipment_list.maintenance: Clean with 70% ethanol; UV lamps tested every 3 months; replace if <80% output.

equipment_list.name: Autoclave
equipment_list.description: Pressurized chamber for sterilization using steam at 121°C, 15 psi, 15-30 min.
equipment_list.use: Sterilization of media and decontamination of waste. Separate autoclaves for clean and used items.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Use biological indicator (Geobacillus stearothermophilus) monthly; autoclave tape each cycle.
equipment_list.maintenance: Daily clean door gasket; weekly clean trays; monthly activate safety valve.

equipment_list.name: Incubators
equipment_list.description: Insulated chamber for stable temperature; BOD incubator for <30°C; CO2 incubator for anaerobes.
equipment_list.use: Separate incubators for each temperature; never overload.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Check temperature daily with calibrated thermometer.
equipment_list.maintenance: Clean and sanitize regularly; disinfect spills immediately.

equipment_list.name: Anaerobic Jar
equipment_list.description: Enclosed system for anaerobic incubation using gas-generating kits.

equipment_list.name: Microwave Oven
equipment_list.maintenance: Clean spills immediately; check door seals.

equipment_list.name: Balances and Gravimetric Diluters
equipment_list.use: Weighing test portions and media components.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Daily check with working weights; calibration every 3-6 months.
equipment_list.maintenance: Clean before each use; do not interchange pan supports.

equipment_list.name: pH Meter
equipment_list.description: Measures pH with accuracy 0.05 units, resolution 0.01 units.
equipment_list.use: Check pH of culture media and reagents.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Calibrate daily with at least two buffers (pH 4.00, 7.00, 10.00); slope should be 95-105%.
equipment_list.maintenance: Rinse electrodes; store in appropriate solution; clean with pepsin HCl if needed.

equipment_list.name: Homogenizers, Blenders and Mixers
equipment_list.description: Peristaltic blender (stomacher), rotary homogenizer (8000-45000 rpm), vibrational mixer (pulsifier).
equipment_list.use: Prepare initial suspension from non-liquid samples.
equipment_list.maintenance: Clean and disinfect after each use; sterilize bowls.

equipment_list.name: Thermostatically controlled Water Baths
equipment_list.use: Incubation at constant temperature, maintenance of molten agar, heat treatment.
equipment_list.maintenance: Use distilled water; clean and disinfect regularly; heat to 80°C for one hour to clean.

equipment_list.name: Media Preparator
equipment_list.description: Equipment for sterilizing large volumes of media.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Temperature and duration checks; calibration of probes.

equipment_list.name: Membrane Filtration Apparatus
equipment_list.description: Vacuum filtration assembly with 0.45 μm membrane.

equipment_list.name: Thermometers
equipment_list.performance_checks: Calibrate reference thermometers every 5 years; three-point verification for working thermometers.

equipment_list.name: Deionizing and Distillation Apparatus
equipment_list.use: Distilled water for solutions and final rinsing.
equipment_list.performance_checks: Conductivity ≤2 μS/cm at 25°C; microbial count ≤10^3 cfu/ml.

equipment_list.name: Refrigerator/Cold Storage Room
equipment_list.description: Storage at 3±2°C for samples, 5±3°C for media.

equipment_list.name: Colony Counters
equipment_list.performance_checks: Manual checks daily; calibration plate monthly.

equipment_list.name: Gas Burner or Electric Bunsen Burners
equipment_list.description: Flame sterilization of loops, forceps, flask mouths.

equipment_list.name: Dispenser for Culture Media and Reagents
Pipettes and Automatic Pipettes and Tips
equipment_list.description: Glass or disposable plastic for volume delivery.

chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.title: Glassware/Plasticware
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.scope: Guidance for sterilization, handling, storage, decontamination and performance testing.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.glassware_types: Borosilicate glass preferred; soft glass not recommended.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.cleaning_procedure: Detergent wash at 70°C, rinse with soft water at 80°C, final distilled water rinse. Chromic acid for stubborn residues. New glassware: soak in 1% HCl overnight.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.test_for_inhibitory_residues: Use Enterobacter aerogenes; difference in counts <15% indicates acceptable.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.sterilization: Dry heat: 170°C for 1h. Moist heat: autoclave 121°C for 15 min.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.sterility_test: Pour PCA into random plates; incubate 37°C for 48h; no growth.
chapter_2_glassware_plasticware.decontamination: Autoclave at 121°C for 30 min in autoclavable bags.

chapter_3_media_reagents_reference_cultu.title: Media/ Reagents and Reference culture
chapter_3_media_reagents_reference_cultu.introduction: Microbiological examinations use a vast variety of culture media. Formulations vary for different microorganisms and tests.

terms_and_definitions.definition: Homogeneous and fully traceable unit produced within one defined production period.
Substrate containing a chromophore/fluorophore group utilizable by bacteria/fungi.
Level of recovery of target microorganism.
Degree of inhibition of non-target microorganisms.
Liquid medium providing favourable conditions for multiplication (e.g., Tryptone soya broth).
Allows multiplication of specific microorganisms while inhibiting others (e.g., Rappaport-Vassiliadis).

quality_assurance.documentation_from_manufacturer: Name, batch number, target pH, expiry date, quality control certificate.
quality_assurance.delivery_acceptance: Check identity, packaging integrity, expiry date.
quality_assurance.handling_dehydrated_media: First-in-first-out; record opening date; discard if caked or discolored.
quality_assurance.laboratory_preparation: Follow manufacturer's instructions; record code, lot number, mass/volume, pH, sterilization conditions.
quality_assurance.water_quality: Purified water (distilled, deionized, reverse osmosis) with conductivity ≤2 μS/cm.
quality_assurance.sterilization: Moist heat (autoclave) or filtration (0.2 μm). F0 value evaluation.
quality_assurance.storage_shelf_life: Plates: 2-4 weeks at 5±3°C; sealed bottles: 3-6 months.
quality_assurance.melting_agar: Heat until melted; cool to 47-50°C; use within 4h.

test_organisms.selection: Reference strains from culture collections (ATCC, MTCC, NCTC, WDCM).

performance_testing_methods.quantitative: Productivity ratio PR = Ns/No ≥0.5 for selective media, ≥0.7 for non-selective.
performance_testing_methods.qualitative_streaking: Growth scored 0,1,2. Target: score 2 and typical morphology.

chapter_4_quality_assurance.title: Quality Assurance: Assuring Quality of Test Results in Microbiology Laboratory
chapter_4_quality_assurance.scope: Procedures for QA/QC in microbiology laboratory.

definitions.Matrix spike: Sample spiked with known organism to check matrix effect.
definitions.Quality Assurance: Management system for planning, implementation, assessment.
definitions.Quality Control: Technical activities measuring attributes against standards.

qc_practices.demonstration_of_capability: Initial DOC before method use; ongoing DOC monthly with single-blind samples; analyst counts within 5% repeatability, 10% reproducibility.
qc_practices.method_blanks: One per batch; if contaminated, discard samples.
qc_practices.sterility_checks: On each new lot of media.
qc_practices.reference_cultures: From accredited providers; maintain purity and viability documentation.
qc_practices.matrix_spike: For difficult matrices; if recovery not expected, re-evaluate.
qc_practices.calibration: All equipment calibrated per NABL guidelines.
qc_practices.control_charts: For autoclave, balances, temperature devices; mean and control limits.
qc_practices.corrective_action_and_root_cause_analysi: Structured problem-solving to identify and eliminate root causes.
qc_practices.qc_acceptance_criteria: For glassware, water (≤1000 cfu/ml, ≤25 μS/cm), membrane filter sterility, diluents, media performance.

chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.title: Good Microbiology Laboratory Practices including Biosafety and Biohazard Management
chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.scope: Safety design, equipment, personnel, aseptic techniques, and waste management.

safety_design.biosafety_levels: BSL-1 and BSL-2 for food safety labs.
safety_design.general_requirements: Separate storage; dedicated air handling; authorized entry; biohazard signs; environmental monitoring.
safety_design.laboratory_design: Unidirectional flow; smooth cleanable surfaces; hand-washing basins; autoclave nearby.

chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.safety_equipment: Biosafety cabinets; autoclaves; centrifuges with sealed buckets; anaerobic jars.
chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.personnel_practices: Proper uniform and PPE (gloves, lab coat, eye protection); no eating/drinking; hand washing; vaccination; accident reporting.
chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.aseptic_techniques: Flame loops; work near Bunsen burner; use sterile pipettes; avoid mouth pipetting; disinfect work surfaces with 70% ethanol.
chapter_5_good_laboratory_practices.biohazard_waste_management: Segregation into yellow (non-chlorinated bags for anatomical, soiled, microbiological waste), white (puncture-proof for sharps), blue (cardboard for glassware). Autoclave to log 6 or disinfect to log 4 before disposal per Biomedical Waste Management Rules 2016.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Aerobic Plate Count (APC)
part_b_food_methods.scope: Applicable to food product categories under FSSAI regulations.
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pour plate or surface plating technique using Plate Count Agar (PCA) incubated at 30±1°C for 72±3h.
part_b_food_methods.equipment: Laminar airflow, hot air oven, autoclave, incubator (30±1°C), water bath (44-47°C), pH meter, petri dishes, pipettes, colony counter.
part_b_food_methods.media: Plate Count Agar (PCA); diluent: peptone salt solution, buffered peptone water.
part_b_food_methods.reference_cultures: Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Pour plate: 1 ml sample + 15-20 ml PCA (44-47°C), mix, solidify, overlay if needed. Surface plating: 0.1 ml spread on dried PCA plates. Incubate inverted at 30±1°C for 72±3h.
part_b_food_methods.calculation: N = ΣC / [V × (n1 + 0.1×n2) × d] where ΣC = sum of colonies, V = volume, n1,n2 = number of dishes, d = dilution.
part_b_food_methods.expression: Results as cfu/g or ml, rounded to two significant figures.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Bacillus cereus
part_b_food_methods.principle: Spread plating on MYP agar (mannitol egg yolk polymyxin). B. cereus produces pink colonies (mannitol-negative) with precipitate zone (lecithinase). Confirmation by haemolysis and biochemical tests.
part_b_food_methods.equipment: Laminar airflow, biosafety cabinet, incubator (30°C), water bath, pH meter, microscope, colony counter.
part_b_food_methods.media: MYP agar, sheep blood agar, polymyxin B, egg yolk emulsion.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Spread 0.1 ml of dilutions on MYP agar; incubate 30°C for 18-24h; reincubate if needed. Select pink colonies with precipitate; confirm by haemolysis on blood agar.
part_b_food_methods.calculation: N = Σa / [V × (n1+0.1×n2) × d] where a = confirmed colonies.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Determination of Campylobacter spp.
part_b_food_methods.principle: Enrichment in Bolton broth (37°C 4-6h then 41.5°C 44h) then plating on mCCDA, incubated microaerobically at 41.5°C for 24h. Confirmation by oxidase, catalase, hippurate hydrolysis, morphology.
part_b_food_methods.media: Bolton broth, mCCDA, Columbia blood agar, oxidase reagent.
part_b_food_methods.reference_cultures: Campylobacter jejuni WDCM 00005, E. coli WDCM 00013.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Three detection procedures based on sample type. Enriched culture streaked on mCCDA; incubate microaerobically at 41.5°C for 44±4h. Typical colonies: grey, metallic sheen.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Coliforms
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pour plate on Violet Red Bile Lactose (VRBL) agar; coliforms ferment lactose producing red-purple colonies with halo. Confirmation in Brilliant Green Lactose Bile Broth (BGBB).
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 1 ml sample + VRBL agar, solidify, overlay. Incubate 24±2h. Count purple-red colonies >0.5 mm. Confirm atypical colonies in BGBB at 30/37°C for 24h; gas formation confirms.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Commercial Sterility Test for Sterilized/UHT Milk / Flavored Milk / Evaporated Milk
part_b_food_methods.principle: Incubate final product at 55±1°C for 7 days; measure pH and acidity. No physical alteration and pH change ≤0.3 or acidity change ≤0.02% lactic acid indicates sterility.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Commercial Sterility Test for Sterilized/UHT Cream
part_b_food_methods.principle: Incubate at 55±1°C for 7 days (or 30°C for 14 days). Acidity ≤0.15% lactic acid, no bulging, no curdling, no off-odour indicates sterility.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Determination of Cronobacter spp. (Enterobacter sakazakii)
part_b_food_methods.scope: Food products, especially powdered infant formula.
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pre-enrichment in BPW (34-38°C, 18h), selective enrichment in Cronobacter Selective Broth (41.5°C, 24h), plating on Chromogenic Cronobacter Isolation (CCI) agar. Blue-green colonies confirmed by biochemical tests (oxidase, citrate, arginine dihydrolase, etc.).
part_b_food_methods.media: BPW, CSB, CCI agar, TSA, biochemical media.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 10g sample +90ml BPW; incubate 34-38°C/18h. Transfer 0.1ml to 10ml CSB; incubate 41.5°C/24h. Streak on CCI; incubate 41.5°C/24h. Blue-green colonies confirmed.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Sulfite Reducing Clostridia based on ISO 15213
part_b_food_methods.principle: Iron sulfite agar; sulfite-reducing clostridia produce black colonies due to iron sulfide formation under anaerobic conditions.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 1 ml sample + molten iron sulfite agar, overlay, incubate anaerobically at 37°C for 24-48h (or 50°C for thermophiles). Black colonies counted. Confirm by respiratory test and spore formation.

part_b_food_methods.title: Methods for Isolation and Identification of Clostridium Perfringens and Clostridium Botulinum and Enumeration of Clostridium Perfringens based on IS 5887-Part 4
part_b_food_methods.principle: C. perfringens: growth on blood agar with haemolysis, Nagler reaction for alpha toxin. C. botulinum: toxin detection by mouse bioassay (not detailed for safety).
part_b_food_methods.media: Cooked meat medium, Willis and Hobbs medium (egg yolk), blood agar with neomycin.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Sample heated at 100°C for 1h in cooked meat medium; incubate overnight. Subculture on egg yolk and blood agar anaerobically at 37°C. Nagler reaction: lecithinase inhibition by antitoxin.
part_b_food_methods.expression: Presence/absence of C. perfringens and C. botulinum; enumeration as cfu/g.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Enterobacteriaceae
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pour plate on Violet Red Bile Glucose Agar (VRBG); Enterobacteriaceae are glucose-fermenting, oxidase-negative.
part_b_food_methods.media: VRBG agar, glucose OF medium, oxidase reagent.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 1 ml sample + VRBG; overlay; incubate 35/37°C for 24h. Pink to red colonies with/without halo. Confirm with oxidase test (negative) and glucose fermentation (positive).

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Escherichia coli based on ISO 16649-2
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pour plate on Tryptone Bile Glucuronide (TBX) agar; β-glucuronidase-positive E. coli produce blue-green colonies at 44°C.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 1 ml sample + TBX; pour plate; incubate at 44°C for 18-24h. Count blue-green colonies.

part_b_food_methods.title: Methods for Isolation, Identification and Enumeration of Escherichia Coli based on IS 5887-Part 1
part_b_food_methods.principle: Spread plate on Tergitol-7 agar or MPN method using MacConkey broth at 44°C. Confirmation by IMViC tests, indole, MR, VP, citrate, urease.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Spread 0.1 ml on Tergitol-7; yellow colonies with yellow zone. Confirm by Gram stain, motility, indole (positive), H2S negative, MR positive, VP negative, citrate negative.
part_b_food_methods.enumeration: Plate count or MPN using MacConkey broth at 44°C for 48h.

part_b_food_methods.title: Detection, Isolation and Identification of Pathogenic E. Coli in Food based on IS 14397
part_b_food_methods.scope: Pathogenic E. coli (EPEC, ETEC, EIEC, EHEC, EAEC).
part_b_food_methods.principle: Presumptive coliform test, then serological identification (O antigens) and confirmation of enterotoxigenicity (Biken test, rabbit ileal loop, cell culture) or invasiveness (Sereny test).
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Enrich in MacConkey broth; test for acid/gas at 44°C (faecal coliforms) and indole. Serotyping. ETEC: Biken test (precipitation line) or Y-1 adrenal cell rounding. EIEC: Sereny test (keratoconjunctivitis in guinea pig). EHEC: sorbitol non-fermenter on SMAC, confirmed by O157:H7 antisera.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Detection and Confirmation of Listeria monocytogenes based on IS: 14988-Part 1
part_b_food_methods.principle: Primary enrichment in Half-Fraser broth (30°C, 24h), secondary in Fraser broth (37°C, 24h), plating on Oxford and PALCAM agar. Confirmation by Gram stain, catalase, motility, haemolysis, CAMP test, carbohydrate utilization.
part_b_food_methods.media: Half-Fraser, Fraser, Oxford agar, PALCAM agar, TSAYE, sheep blood agar.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 25g sample +225ml Half-Fraser; incubate 30°C/24h. Transfer 0.1ml to Fraser; incubate 37°C/24h. Streak on Oxford and PALCAM; incubate 30-37°C for 48h. Typical small colonies with black halo. Confirm: Gram-positive rods, tumbling motility, catalase positive, β-haemolysis, CAMP positive with S. aureus, acid from rhamnose (positive) not xylose.
part_b_food_methods.expression: L. monocytogenes present/absent per 25g or ml.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Detection and Confirmation of Listeria monocytogenes based on ISO 11290-1
part_b_food_methods.principle: Similar to IS method but uses Agar Listeria Ottaviani and Agosti (ALOA) as chromogenic medium; blue-green colonies with opaque halo.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Same enrichment; streaking on ALOA and optional second medium. Blue-green colonies with halo are presumptive. Confirmation: as above.

part_b_food_methods.title: Detection and Confirmation of Salmonella based on IS: 5887 Part 3
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pre-enrichment in BPW (35/37°C, 16-20h), selective enrichment in RV broth (42°C) and selenite-cystine broth (35-37°C), plating on Brilliant Green Agar (BGA) and second selective medium. Confirmation by TSI, LIA, urease, lysine decarboxylase, serology.
part_b_food_methods.media: BPW, RV broth, selenite-cystine broth, BGA, TSI, LIA, urea agar.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 25g sample +225ml BPW; incubate 35-37°C/16-20h. Transfer 0.1ml to RV (42°C) and 1ml to selenite-cystine (35-37°C) both for 24h. Streak on BGA; incubate 35-37°C/24h. Typical colonies: red with red surrounding. Confirm: TSI red slant/yellow butt, H2S positive (black), lysine decarboxylase positive, urease negative, O and H antisera agglutination.

part_b_food_methods.title: Detection and Confirmation of Salmonella based on ISO:6579-I
part_b_food_methods.principle: Similar but uses MSRV or RVS broth and MKTTn broth, plating on XLD agar.
part_b_food_methods.media: BPW, RVS, MKTTn, XLD agar, TSI, LIA.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 25g +225ml BPW; 34-38°C/18±2h. Transfer 0.1ml to RVS (41.5°C) and 1ml to MKTTn (37°C); incubate 24±3h. Streak on XLD; incubate 37°C/24h. Typical colonies: black centre with reddish zone. Confirmation as above.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Detection and Confirmation of Shigella based on ISO: 21567
part_b_food_methods.principle: Enrichment in Shigella broth with novobiocin (41.5°C anaerobic, 16-20h), plating on MacConkey, XLD, Hektoen enteric agars. Confirmation by biochemical tests (TSI, urease, lysine decarboxylase, ornithine decarboxylase, indole, etc.) and serotyping.
part_b_food_methods.media: Shigella broth, MacConkey, XLD, Hektoen, nutrient agar, TSI, urea broth, decarboxylase media.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 25g sample +225ml Shigella broth; incubate anaerobically at 41.5°C/16-20h. Streak on selective agars; incubate 37°C/20-24h. Typical colonies: colourless on MacConkey, translucent red/cerise on XLD, green on Hektoen. Confirm: TSI alkaline slant/acid butt, no gas, no H2S, urease negative, lysine decarboxylase negative, ornithine decarboxylase positive only for S. sonnei. Serotyping with polyvalent Shigella antisera.
part_b_food_methods.expression: Shigella spp. present/absent per 25g or ml.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Detection and Confirmation of Shigella based on IS 5887-Part 7
part_b_food_methods.principle: Pre-enrichment in nutrient broth, selective enrichment in tetrathionate and selenite F broths, plating on DCA and MacConkey. Biochemical and serological confirmation.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Similar to ISO method but using different media. Confirmation includes Gram stain, oxidase, Hugh-Leifson, indole, citrate, carbohydrate fermentation.
part_b_food_methods.expression: Shigella spp. present/absent per 25g or ml.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Coagulase Positive Staphylococcus based on ISO 6888-1/AMD 1 and IS 5887-Part 8 (Sec 1)
part_b_food_methods.principle: Spread plating on Baird-Parker agar; coagulase-positive staphylococci produce black colonies (tellurite reduction) with clear halo (lecithinase). Confirmation by coagulase test.
part_b_food_methods.media: Baird-Parker agar (BPA), brain heart infusion broth, rabbit plasma.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Spread 0.1 ml of dilutions on BPA; incubate at 35-37°C for 24±2h, then reincubate for further 24h. Typical colonies: shiny black/grey with clear zone. Confirm: coagulase test (tube method) – clot formation.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Coagulase Positive Staphylococcus based on ISO 6888-2 and IS 5887-Part 8 (Sec 2)
part_b_food_methods.principle: Enrichment in cooked meat salt medium, then plating on BPA and blood agar. Confirmation by coagulase test.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Enrich sample in cooked meat salt medium at 37°C/18-24h. Streak on BPA (30h) and blood agar (18-24h). Typical colonies: black with halo on BPA, golden yellow with haemolysis on blood agar. Confirmation by coagulase.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Determination of Vibrio cholera and Vibrio parahaemolyticus
part_b_food_methods.principle: Enrichment in alkaline saline peptone water (ASPW) at 37°C or 41.5°C depending on product. Streak on TCBS agar; V. cholerae: yellow colonies (sucrose positive); V. parahaemolyticus: green colonies (sucrose negative). Confirmation by oxidase, halotolerance, lysine decarboxylase, etc., and PCR for virulence genes (tdh, trh).
part_b_food_methods.media: ASPW, TCBS, saline nutrient agar, LDC, ADH, oxidase reagent.
part_b_food_methods.procedure: 25g sample +225ml ASPW; incubate at appropriate temperature for 6h then transfer 1ml to fresh ASPW for 18h at 41.5°C. Streak on TCBS; incubate 37°C/24h. Typical colonies: yellow (V. cholerae) or green (V. parahaemolyticus). Confirm by oxidase positive, growth in 0% NaCl (V. cholerae) or 6% NaCl (V. parahaemolyticus), LDC positive, ADH negative. Optional PCR for ctx, tdh, trh.

part_b_food_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Yeast and Mould
part_b_food_methods.principle: Spread or pour plate on Chloramphenicol Yeast Glucose Agar (CGYEA); chloramphenicol inhibits bacteria. Incubate at 25±1°C for 3-5 days.
part_b_food_methods.media: CGYEA, sodium propionate (to inhibit moulds if only yeast count needed).
part_b_food_methods.procedure: Spread 0.1 ml or pour 1 ml of dilutions on CGYEA; incubate 25°C/3-5 days. Yeast: smooth, moist colonies; mould: fuzzy, filamentous.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Aerobic Microbial count/Standard Plate Count
part_c_water_methods.principle: Pour plate on Plate Count Agar (PCA); incubate at 37°C for 24h (mesophilic) and 20-22°C for 72h (psychrotrophic).
part_c_water_methods.procedure: 1 ml water sample + PCA; pour plate; incubate.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Escherichia coli and Coliform
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration on Chromogenic Coliform Agar (CCA). E. coli: dark blue to violet (β-glucuronidase positive); coliforms: pink to red (β-galactosidase positive). Confirmation by oxidase negative.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter water sample through 0.45 μm membrane; place on CCA; incubate 36±2°C for 18-24h. Count coloured colonies. Oxidase test on presumptive colonies.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Enumeration of Coliform (Alternative method)
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration on Violet Red Bile Lactose (VRBL) agar; coliforms produce purplish red colonies with precipitated bile.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter sample, place on VRBL, incubate 36±1°C for 24±2h.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Determination of Enterococci (Faecal Streptococci)
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration on Slanetz and Bartley medium (red colonies), confirm on Bile Aesculin Azide agar (tan to black colonies due to aesculin hydrolysis).
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter sample, place on Slanetz & Bartley; incubate 36±2°C/44±4h. Transfer membrane to Bile Aesculin Azide agar; incubate 44±0.5°C/2h.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Enterococci (Faecal Streptococci) (Alternative method)
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration on Ethyl Violet Azide Dextrose Agar (dark red colonies), confirmation by Gram stain and growth on MacConkey at 44°C.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter, place on EVAD agar; incubate 37°C/48h. Subculture on MacConkey at 44°C; pink colonies, Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains confirm.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Salmonella
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration, pre-enrichment in BPW, selective enrichment in RVS and MKTTn, plating on XLD and BGA. Confirmation by biochemical and serological tests.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter 250 ml water, place filter in 50 ml BPW; incubate 36±2°C/16-20h. Transfer 0.1ml to RVS (41.5°C) and 1ml to MKTTn (37°C); incubate 24h. Streak on XLD and BGA; incubate 36±2°C/24h. Confirmation: TSI, lysine decarboxylase, urease, serology.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Shigella
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration, enrichment in nutrient broth, then selenite-F and tetrathionate broths, plating on DCA and MacConkey. Confirmation by biochemical tests and serotyping.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter 250 ml, place filter in 50 ml nutrient broth; incubate 37°C/18-24h. Transfer 1ml to selenite-F and tetrathionate; incubate 37°C/24h. Streak on DCA; incubate 37°C/24-48h. Typical colonies: opaque with ground-glass appearance. Confirm: TSI, urease, citrate, indole, carbohydrate fermentation, serotyping.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
part_c_water_methods.principle: Filtration, enrichment in asparagine proline broth (37°C/48h), plating on milk agar with cetrimide (42°C/24h). Blue-green pigmented colonies with casein hydrolysis and fluorescence under UV are confirmed.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter, place filter in 50 ml asparagine proline broth; incubate 37°C/48h. Subculture on milk agar; incubate 42°C/24h. Look for blue-green colonies, clearing (casein hydrolysis), fluorescence under UV. Confirm by oxidase, catalase, oxidative metabolism.
part_c_water_methods.expression: P. aeruginosa present/absent per X ml.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Yeast & Mould
part_c_water_methods.principle: Membrane filtration on Chloramphenicol Yeast Glucose Agar (CGYEA); incubate at 25±1°C for 3-5 days.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter 250 ml water, place filter on CGYEA; incubate 25°C/3-5 days. Examine for yeast (smooth, moist) and mould (fuzzy) colonies.
part_c_water_methods.expression: Yeast and mould present/absent per X ml.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Sulphite-Reducing anaerobes (Clostridia)
part_c_water_methods.principle: Heat shock (75°C/15 min) then inoculation into Differential Reinforced Clostridial Medium (DRCM); anaerobic incubation at 37°C for 44±4h. Blackening indicates sulphite reduction.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Heat 100 ml sample at 75°C/15 min. Add 50 ml to 50 ml double-strength DRCM; incubate anaerobically at 37°C/44±4h. Black colour = positive.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Vibrio parahaemolyticus
part_c_water_methods.principle: Enrichment in glucose-salt-teepol broth, plating on TCBS (green colonies). Confirmation by oxidase, halotolerance (growth in 8% NaCl, not 10%), lysine decarboxylase positive, ornithine decarboxylase positive, Kanagawa test (thermostable direct haemolysin).
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter sample, place filter in 50 ml glucose-salt-teepol broth; incubate 37°C overnight. Streak on TCBS; incubate 37°C/18h. Green colonies. Confirm by oxidase, growth in 8% NaCl, no growth in 0% and 10% NaCl, LDC+, ODC+, Kanagawa positive (β-haemolysis on Wagatsuma agar).
part_c_water_methods.expression: V. parahaemolyticus present/absent per X ml.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Vibrio cholerae
part_c_water_methods.principle: Enrichment in alkaline peptone water, plating on TCBS (yellow colonies) and bile salt agar. Confirmation by oxidase, motility, halotolerance (growth in 0% NaCl, not in 8%), lysine decarboxylase positive, serology with polyvalent O1 antiserum.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter, place filter in 50 ml alkaline peptone water; incubate 37°C overnight. Streak on TCBS and BSA; incubate 37°C overnight. Yellow colonies on TCBS. Confirm: oxidase positive, motile, growth in 0% NaCl, no growth in 8% NaCl, LDC+, ODC+, indole positive, serology positive with O1 or O139 antisera.
part_c_water_methods.expression: V. cholerae present/absent per X ml.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Staphylococcus aureus
part_c_water_methods.principle: Enrichment in cooked salt meat medium, plating on Baird-Parker agar and blood agar. Confirmation by coagulase test.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter, place filter in 50 ml cooked salt meat medium; incubate 37°C overnight. Streak on BPA (30h) and blood agar (18-24h). Black colonies with halo on BPA, golden yellow with haemolysis on blood agar. Confirm by coagulase test.
part_c_water_methods.expression: S. aureus present/absent per X ml.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Viruses (Enterovirus and Hepatitis A Virus)
part_c_water_methods.principle: Concentration by filtration (100 L) using positively charged or nitrocellulose membrane, elution with urea-arginine phosphate buffer, RNA extraction (CTAB), RT-PCR for HAV and enterovirus.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter 100 L water; elute with U-APB; concentrate. Extract RNA; synthesize cDNA; PCR with HAV and EV primers. Agarose gel electrophoresis; 155 bp for EV, 225 bp for HAV.
part_c_water_methods.expression: Entero virus = Present/Absent; HAV virus = Present/Absent.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of MS2 Phage in Water by Enrichment Spot Assay Technique
part_c_water_methods.principle: Enrichment with host E. coli Famp, then spot assay on tryptone agar. Lysis zone indicates presence of MS2 phage.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: To 1000 ml water add E. coli culture, CaCl2, tryptone enrichment broth, antibiotics; incubate overnight. Spot 10 μl onto tryptone spot agar with host lawn; incubate overnight; observe clearing.

part_c_water_methods.title: Method for Detection of Giardia and Cryptosporidium - Method A
part_c_water_methods.principle: Concentration using Envirochek or Filta-Max filters, immunomagnetic separation (IMS), staining with FITC-labelled monoclonal antibodies and DAPI, epifluorescence/DIC microscopy.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Filter water; elute; IMS to capture oocysts/cysts; stain with FITC-mAb and DAPI. Examine under epifluorescence microscope. Cryptosporidium: apple-green spherical oocysts (4-6 μm), 2-4 sky-blue nuclei with DAPI. Giardia: apple-green ovoid cysts (8-12 μm × 7-10 μm). Confirm with DIC morphology.
part_c_water_methods.expression: Number of oocysts/cysts per volume or 'not detected'.

part_c_water_methods.title: Isolation and Identification of Giardia and Cryptosporidium - Method B
part_c_water_methods.principle: Alternative concentration by calcium carbonate flocculation or iron(II) sulfate flocculation or membrane filtration, then IMS and staining as in Method A.
part_c_water_methods.procedure: Flocculation of 10 L water with CaCl2/NaHCO3/NaOH; settle; dissolve floc with sulfamic acid; centrifuge; IMS; staining. Or ferrous sulfate flocculation. Then microscopy as Method A.

overview.definition: Foodborne illness is a common, costly, sometimes life threatening—yet largely preventable—public health problem.
overview.causes: Bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Listeria, E. coli) and viruses (e.g., norovirus, hepatitis A).
overview.symptoms: Range from mild discomfort to serious, life-threatening illness.
overview.us_annual_cases: Approximately 48 million cases per year (CDC estimate).

pathogens.name: E. coli
pathogens.description: Escherichia coli is a major bacteria species that can live in human intestines. Some strains are harmless, but others cause severe illness.
pathogens.transmission: Contaminated food or water. Often involved in major outbreaks worldwide.
pathogens.symptoms: Varies by strain; can cause severe illness including bloody diarrhea and kidney failure (e.g., O157:H7).
prevention: Practice safe food handling
Cook meats thoroughly
Avoid unpasteurized (raw) milk and unpasteurized juices such as fresh apple cider

pathogens.name: Norovirus
pathogens.description: Most common cause of illness from contaminated food or water in the US. Also spreads easily person-to-person.
pathogens.transmission: Contaminated food or water, direct contact with infected person.
pathogens.symptoms: Onset within 1-2 days (as few as 12 hours). Projectile vomiting often first symptom, along with diarrhea, cramps, headache, mild fever, muscle aches.
prevention: Practice safe food handling
Good handwashing

pathogens.name: Salmonella
pathogens.description: Causes two kinds of illness: Salmonella gastroenteritis and enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid).

subtypes.name: Salmonella gastroenteritis
subtypes.symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, fever. Lasts a couple of days to a week.
subtypes.transmission: Many foods: meats, eggs, fruits, vegetables, spices, nuts.

subtypes.name: Enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid)
subtypes.symptoms: High fever, diarrhea or constipation, aches, headache, drowsiness.
subtypes.transmission: Sewage-contaminated drinking water. Majority of US cases are travelers infected outside the US.
subtypes.mortality: Up to 10% of untreated cases may die.

prevention: Cook foods thoroughly
Good handwashing
Keep raw foods separated from cooked foods
Maintain correct food temperatures
Get vaccinated against typhoid fever if traveling to endemic areas

pathogens.name: Campylobacter
pathogens.description: One of the most common causes of foodborne illness in the US. Most cases are sporadic, not part of outbreaks.
pathogens.transmission: Contaminated water, unpasteurized milk or cheese, raw or undercooked poultry (and sometimes other meats and seafood).
pathogens.symptoms: Onset within 2-5 days, lasts up to 10 days. Gastrointestinal symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), cramps, fever. Can spread to bloodstream causing life-threatening infection.
prevention: Cook meat (especially poultry) thoroughly
Practice safe food handling and good handwashing
Avoid raw or unpasteurized milk and cheese

pathogens.name: Hepatitis A
pathogens.description: Illness caused by Hepatitis A virus. Usually mild and self-resolving.
pathogens.transmission: Eating or drinking contaminated food or water. Foods often linked: contaminated water, shellfish, salads.
pathogens.symptoms: Onset 2-4 weeks after consumption, lasts 1-2 weeks. Fever, low appetite, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle aches, jaundice (yellowing of eyes and skin).
prevention: Good handwashing

pathogens.name: Listeria (Listeriosis)
pathogens.description: Not common, but one of the leading causes of death from foodborne illness.

subtypes.name: Non-invasive listeriosis
subtypes.symptoms: Mild to intense nausea, vomiting, aches, fever, sometimes diarrhea. Usually resolves itself.

subtypes.name: Invasive listeriosis
subtypes.symptoms: Infection spreads beyond gut to blood or brain. Can cause blood infection, meningitis, other potentially fatal problems. In pregnant women: miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm labor, severe illness or death in newborn.

prevention: Good handwashing
Keep refrigerator clean and at 40°F (4°C)
Separate raw foods from cooked foods
Avoid unpasteurized (raw) milk and cheese

section_1.title: Foodborne disease: Epidemiology and disease burden

chapter_1.title: Estimates of global disease burden associated with foodborne pathogens
chapter_1.authors: Sara M. Pires and Brecht Devleesschauwer

sections.heading: Why is it important to estimate the burden of foodborne disease?
sections.content: To address 21st-century food safety challenges, an integrated, multidisciplinary, science-based, risk-based approach is needed. Burden of foodborne disease studies serve three purposes: (1) prioritize food safety as an issue within a country, (2) prioritize specific hazards, and (3) monitor trends and evaluate interventions.

subsections.heading: Burden of disease metrics
subsections.content: Metrics include incidence, mortality, Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), which combine years of life lost due to premature death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD).

subsections.heading: Reconstructing the 'burden-of-illness pyramid'
subsections.content: Underreporting is common; only a fraction of cases are captured by surveillance. Multiplier approaches adjust for under-ascertainment.

subsections.heading: Attributing illnesses to foodborne transmission
subsections.content: Illnesses may be transmitted via multiple routes (food, water, animal contact, person-to-person). Source attribution methods include outbreak data, comparative exposure assessment, microbial subtyping, and expert elicitation.

sections.heading: Estimates of the global burden of foodborne disease

subsections.heading: Foodborne Disease Burden Epidemiology Reference Group (2006–15)
subsections.content: WHO established FERG to estimate the global burden of foodborne diseases. Over 100 experts collaborated.

subsections.heading: Global and regional burden of foodborne diseases, 2010
subsections.content: Full estimates published in 2015. Key findings: 31 foodborne hazards (11 diarrheal agents, 7 invasive infectious, 10 parasitic, 3 chemicals) caused 600 million illnesses and 420,000 deaths annually. Children under 5 bear 40% of the burden. Norovirus, Campylobacter, and enteropathogenic E. coli are leading causes.

subsections.heading: Estimates of the national burden of foodborne disease
subsections.content: National studies in Netherlands, France, UK, US, Australia, New Zealand, and others have been conducted. Methodologies vary but increasingly align with WHO FERG framework.

sections.heading: National and global burden of foodborne disease: What is next?
sections.content: Future priorities: harmonize national methods, include more hazards, improve source attribution, incorporate climate change and emerging pathogens, and build capacity in low- and middle-income countries for routine disease surveillance and burden estimation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.content: Burden estimates are essential for risk-based food safety policy. International collaboration and methodological improvements continue to refine these estimates.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Risk assessment provides a systematic framework to evaluate the probability and severity of adverse health effects from foodborne hazards.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content: Microbiological risk assessment (MRA) is part of risk analysis (along with risk management and risk communication). It is used to support food safety decisions.

sections.heading: Managing microbial food safety risks
sections.content: Risk management includes setting food safety objectives (FSOs), performance criteria, and process criteria.

sections.heading: The risk assessment framework
sections.content: Four steps: hazard identification, exposure assessment, hazard characterization, risk characterization.

sections.heading: Risk assessment in practice
sections.content: Examples: risk assessments for Salmonella in eggs and broilers, Listeria in ready-to-eat foods, Campylobacter in poultry.

sections.heading: Model harmonization and knowledge exchange
sections.content: Initiatives like the OECD's Foodborne Disease Burden model and the FAO/WHO’s risk assessment tools promote standardization.

sections.heading: The use of sequencing data
sections.content: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) enhances source attribution and allows more precise risk assessment.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Outbreak investigations identify sources and prevent further illness. They also provide data for source attribution and prevention strategies.

sections.heading: Investigation process
sections.content: Steps: detection, hypothesis generation, epidemiological studies (cohort, case-control), environmental and laboratory investigation, traceback, and control measures.

sections.heading: Lessons learned from FBDOs
sections.content: Outbreaks reveal gaps in food safety systems and emerging hazards (e.g., E. coli O157 in leafy greens, Cyclospora in produce).

sections.heading: Source attribution
sections.content: Outbreak data are used to estimate which foods cause most illnesses for each pathogen.

sections.heading: National surveillance systems
sections.content: PulseNet (USA) for molecular subtyping, FoodNet for active surveillance, and CaliciNet for noroviruses.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content: Outbreak investigations remain critical to public health and inform prevention policies.

chapter_4.title: Molecular epidemiology of foodborne pathogens
chapter_4.authors: Brittany Rife Magalis and Marco Salemi

sections.heading: Historical lessons: Reconstructing the past of a pathogen
sections.content: Phylogenetic analysis using genome sequences can trace evolutionary history, emergence, and spread of pathogens (e.g., Salmonella Typhi, Vibrio cholerae).

sections.heading: Joining forces: Integrative approaches to determining the impact of control measures
sections.content: Combining epidemiological data with pathogen genomics allows evaluation of interventions (e.g., vaccination, sanitation).

sections.heading: Tracing origins: Phylogenetic clues into the outbreak source
sections.content: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) provides high resolution for linking clinical, food, and environmental isolates during outbreaks.

sections.heading: Adaptive insights: A whole-genome approach to identifying selection pressure
sections.content: Genomic analyses identify adaptive mutations in virulence factors, antimicrobial resistance, and host adaptation.

sections.heading: Conflict resolution: Overcoming complications of horizontal transfer and recombination in phylogenetic reconstruction
sections.content: Recombination and horizontal gene transfer can confound phylogenetic trees. Recombination detection methods and robust tree-building approaches (e.g., Bayesian phylogenetics) are used.

sections.heading: Closing remarks
sections.content: Genomic epidemiology is revolutionizing foodborne disease surveillance and outbreak response.

chapter_5.title: Salmonella infections
chapter_5.authors: Radhika Gharpure, Jessica M. Healy, A.C. Lauer, and Robert V. Tauxe

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Salmonella is a leading cause of bacterial foodborne illness worldwide. Non-typhoidal Salmonella causes gastroenteritis; typhoidal Salmonella (Typhi, Paratyphi) causes enteric fever.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 6–72 hours. Symptoms: diarrhea (often bloody), fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting. Usually self-limiting (4–7 days). Invasive disease in immunocompromised, young, elderly.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Acute gastroenteritis; enteric fever (prolonged fever, headache, constipation or diarrhea, rose spots).

chapter_6.title: Clostridium perfringens gastroenteritis
chapter_6.authors: Santos Garcia, Norma Heredia, Ronald G. Labbé, and Vijay K. Juneja

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: C. perfringens is a spore-forming anaerobic bacterium that produces enterotoxin (CPE) during sporulation in the intestine, causing diarrhea and cramps.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 8–24 hours; symptoms: abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, nausea (vomiting rare). Self-limiting (24 hours).

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Gram-positive rod, forms subterminal spores. Types A–E; type A causes food poisoning. CPE is a 35 kDa protein.

sections.heading: Factors affecting growth
sections.content: Temperature: 15–50°C (optimum 43–47°C). Generation time as short as 7 minutes. Spores heat-resistant (survive cooking).

sections.heading: Detection and enumeration
sections.content: Selective media: TSC (tryptose sulfite cycloserine) agar. Confirmation by lack of motility, lactose fermentation, gelatin liquefaction, reverse CAMP test. Enterotoxin detected by ELISA or RPLA.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Rapid cooling of cooked foods (<4°C), avoid prolonged holding at room temperature, reheat to >74°C.

chapter_7.title: Vibrios
chapter_7.authors: Anita C. Wright and Naim Montazeri

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Vibrio species are naturally present in marine environments. Pathogenic species: V. cholerae (cholera), V. parahaemolyticus, V. vulnificus.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Cholera: profuse watery diarrhea (rice-water stools), vomiting, rapid dehydration. V. parahaemolyticus: watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea. V. vulnificus: primary septicemia in immunocompromised (especially liver disease).

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Gram-negative curved rods, halophilic (require NaCl). Produce various toxins (cholera toxin, thermostable direct hemolysin).

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish (oysters, clams, mussels) and exposure of wounds to seawater.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Post-harvest processing (high pressure, freezing, mild heat), refrigeration, cooking, and consumer education for high-risk populations.

chapter_9.title: Campylobacter
chapter_9.authors: Sabine Kienesberger and Guillermo Ignacio Perez-Perez

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Campylobacter jejuni is the most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis worldwide. Also C. coli, C. fetus, C. upsaliensis.

sections.heading: Clinical infection
sections.content: Incubation 2–5 days. Symptoms: diarrhea (often bloody), fever, abdominal pain, nausea. Usually self-limiting (7-10 days). Guillain-Barré syndrome is a rare but serious sequela.

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Microaerophilic, curved Gram-negative rods, motile. Thermotolerant (grow at 42°C).

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, contaminated water, direct contact with animals.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Proper cooking of poultry, pasteurization of milk, hand hygiene, prevention of cross-contamination.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Yersinia enterocolitica and Y. pseudotuberculosis cause yersiniosis, a zoonotic infection.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 4–6 days. Symptoms: enterocolitis (abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever). May mimic appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis).

sections.heading: Reservoirs and exposure
sections.content: Pigs are primary reservoir for pathogenic Y. enterocolitica. Transmission via undercooked pork, raw milk, and contaminated water.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Good slaughter hygiene, cooking pork thoroughly, pasteurization of milk, safe water.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis, a severe invasive disease with high mortality (20–30%), especially in pregnant women, elderly, and immunocompromised.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 3–70 days. In pregnant women: mild flu-like illness but can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal sepsis. In others: meningitis, septicemia, encephalitis.

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Gram-positive rod, psychrotrophic (grows at refrigeration temperatures). Produces hemolysin (listeriolysin O).

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Ready-to-eat foods: soft cheeses, deli meats, smoked seafood, raw produce.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Refrigeration alone is insufficient; heat treatment (pasteurization) kills the organism. Post-processing contamination is a major risk. Environmental monitoring and HACCP in processing plants.

chapter_12.title: Shigella
chapter_12.authors: Amanda G. Garcia-Williams, Naeemah Logan, and Zachary A. Marsh

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Shigella causes shigellosis (bacillary dysentery). Transmission is fecal-oral, often via contaminated food or water, and person-to-person.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 12–96 hours. Symptoms: watery diarrhea, fever, abdominal cramps, blood and mucus in stools. Severe in children and malnourished.

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Contaminated food (salads, raw vegetables, seafood), water, and infected food handlers.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Hand hygiene, safe water, proper sanitation, and exclusion of ill food handlers.

chapter_13.title: Aeromonas and Plesiomonas
chapter_13.authors: Christopher J. Grim and Chris A. Whitehouse

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Aeromonas spp. and Plesiomonas shigelloides are associated with water and seafood. Causative role in gastroenteritis is debated but well-documented in some outbreaks.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting; occasionally dysentery. Self-limiting.

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Contaminated water, seafood (especially raw shellfish), and untreated drinking water.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Adequate cooking, safe water treatment, and hygiene.

chapter_14.title: Brucellosis
chapter_14.authors: Curtis L. Fritz and Duc J. Vugia

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Brucella species cause brucellosis, a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals to humans via unpasteurized dairy products or direct contact.

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Incubation 5 days to several months. Symptoms: undulant fever, sweats, malaise, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly. Chronic infection possible.

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Gram-negative coccobacilli; facultative intracellular.

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Unpasteurized milk and cheese (especially soft cheeses), raw meat, contact with infected animals.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Pasteurization of dairy products, animal vaccination (livestock), personal protective equipment for at-risk workers.

chapter_15.title: Cronobacter species
chapter_15.authors: Hyein Jang, Gopal Gopinath, Flavia Negrete, Leah Weinstein, Angelika Lehner, Séamus Fanning, and Ben D. Tall

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Cronobacter (formerly Enterobacter sakazakii) causes rare but severe neonatal infections: meningitis, necrotizing enterocolitis, bacteremia. High mortality (40–80%).

sections.heading: Clinical features
sections.content: Occurs primarily in infants, especially premature or low birth weight.

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.content: Gram-negative motile rods. Thermotolerance and desiccation resistance allow survival in powdered infant formula.

sections.heading: Exposure pathways
sections.content: Powdered infant formula is the main vehicle. Contamination may occur at processing or during reconstitution.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
sections.content: Strict hygiene in formula production, using hot water (≥70°C) to reconstitute formula, and refrigerating unused formula promptly.

content_chunks.heading: CHAPTER 1: Estimates of global disease burden associated with foodborne pathogens
content_chunks.text: Sara M. Pires and Brecht Devleesschauwer. Why is it important to estimate the burden of foodborne disease? To address food safety challenges of the 21st century, there is need for an integrated, multidisciplinary, system-based approach informed by the best available science. Limited resources need to be utilized to address the most important issues. Food safety systems are evolving from responsive to preventive and risk-based systems. Central to this is quantitative understanding of risks and burden of disease. Burden studies serve three purposes: (1) provide overview of societal impact of major foodborne hazards to prioritize food safety as an issue; (2) hazard-specific estimates allow prioritizing specific food safety issues; (3) over time, they allow monitoring trends and evaluating interventions. Estimating burden is challenging because: over 250 agents (bacteria, viruses, parasites, chemicals) may contaminate food; health effects are complex, beyond acute gastroenteritis, affecting all organ systems on different time scales (e.g., Campylobacter can cause Guillain-Barré syndrome or reactive arthritis; Toxoplasma gondii can cause severe neurological sequelae in unborn child).

content_chunks.heading: Methodological considerations
content_chunks.text: Burden of disease metrics: Often measured in Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), which sum years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD). Reconstructing the 'burden-of-illness pyramid': many cases are mild or unreported; only a fraction seek healthcare, get diagnosed, and reported. Attributing illnesses to foodborne transmission: requires source attribution models to estimate proportion of disease burden caused by food versus water, environment, animal contact, or person-to-person. Estimates of global burden of foodborne disease: Foodborne Disease Burden Epidemiology Reference Group (FERG) 2006-2015. Global and regional burden for 2010: first comprehensive estimates of foodborne disease burden worldwide. National burden estimates: many countries have conducted their own studies. Next steps: improving data quality, integrating whole-genome sequencing, and routine burden estimation within national surveillance systems.

faq.question: What is food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning (also called foodborne illness) is a sickness caused by eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites, or toxins. It typically causes stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea.

faq.question: How common is food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning is very common. The WHO estimates that 600 million people worldwide — nearly 1 in 10 — fall ill after eating contaminated food each year, resulting in 420,000 deaths annually.

faq.question: Is food poisoning contagious?
faq.answer: Some forms of food poisoning caused by viruses (like norovirus or hepatitis A) can spread from person to person through poor hand hygiene. Bacterial food poisoning (like Salmonella or E. coli) is generally not directly contagious but can spread through contaminated surfaces or food.

faq.question: What causes food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning is caused by: bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Campylobacter, Staphylococcus aureus), viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A, rotavirus), parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma), and natural or chemical toxins (from mushrooms, shellfish, or pesticides).

faq.question: Which foods are most likely to cause food poisoning?
faq.answer: High-risk foods include: raw or undercooked poultry, meat, and seafood; raw eggs; unpasteurized milk and dairy products; unwashed fruits and vegetables; cooked rice left at room temperature; deli meats; raw sprouts; and pre-packaged salads.

faq.question: Can drinking water cause food poisoning?
faq.answer: Yes. Contaminated water can carry bacteria, viruses, or parasites that cause foodborne illness. This is especially common in areas with poor sanitation. Always drink clean, treated, or bottled water when traveling to high-risk regions.

faq.question: Can food poisoning happen from restaurant food?
faq.answer: Yes. Restaurants are a common source of food poisoning due to improper food handling, undercooking, cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods, or food being kept at unsafe temperatures. Buffets and street food can carry higher risk if hygiene standards are not maintained.

faq.question: What is cross-contamination in food safety?
faq.answer: Cross-contamination occurs when harmful bacteria or allergens transfer from one food (usually raw) to another (cooked or ready-to-eat) via hands, surfaces, or utensils. For example, cutting raw chicken and then using the same knife for vegetables without washing it.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
faq.answer: Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, abdominal pain, fever, chills, headache, and fatigue. Symptoms can range from mild to severe depending on the contaminant and the person's health.

faq.question: How soon after eating do food poisoning symptoms start?
faq.answer: The onset time varies by cause: Staphylococcus toxins cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours; Salmonella takes 6–48 hours; E. coli 3–4 days; Listeria 1–4 weeks. Most common cases begin within 2–6 hours of eating contaminated food.

faq.question: How long does food poisoning last?
faq.answer: Most mild to moderate cases of food poisoning resolve within 1–3 days. More serious infections (like Listeria or E. coli O157:H7) can last a week or longer and may require medical treatment.

faq.question: What does food poisoning feel like?
faq.answer: Food poisoning typically starts with sudden nausea and stomach cramps, followed by vomiting and/or diarrhea. You may also feel weak, feverish, or have chills. The discomfort can be intense but usually improves within a few days.

faq.question: Can food poisoning cause a fever?
faq.answer: Yes. A mild to moderate fever is common with food poisoning, especially bacterial infections. A high fever (above 38.5°C / 101.5°F) that persists may indicate a more serious infection and warrants medical attention.

faq.question: How is food poisoning treated at home?
faq.answer: Most mild cases can be managed at home by: resting, staying hydrated with water or oral rehydration solutions (ORS), avoiding solid food until vomiting stops, then gradually reintroducing bland foods (toast, rice, bananas), and avoiding dairy, caffeine, alcohol, and fatty foods until recovery.

faq.question: Should I take antibiotics for food poisoning?
faq.answer: Not usually. Most food poisoning cases are caused by viruses or self-limiting bacterial infections that resolve on their own. Antibiotics are only prescribed for certain severe bacterial infections (like Listeria or Salmonella in vulnerable patients) and must be recommended by a doctor.

faq.question: What should I eat and drink when recovering from food poisoning?
faq.answer: Start with clear fluids like water, oral rehydration solution, or diluted fruit juice. Once vomiting settles, eat bland, easy-to-digest foods such as toast, crackers, plain rice, boiled potatoes, and bananas (the BRAT diet). Avoid spicy, fatty, or dairy-rich foods until fully recovered.

faq.question: Should I stop diarrhea with medication during food poisoning?
faq.answer: It is generally better to let diarrhea run its course, as it helps the body flush out toxins. Anti-diarrheal medications like loperamide can be used cautiously for short-term relief in mild cases, but should be avoided if you have bloody diarrhea or a high fever. Always consult a doctor first.

faq.question: How important is hydration during food poisoning?
faq.answer: Hydration is the most critical part of recovery. Vomiting and diarrhea cause rapid fluid and electrolyte loss, which can lead to dehydration. Drink small sips of water or ORS frequently. Signs of dangerous dehydration include dry mouth, dizziness, no urination, and sunken eyes.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor for food poisoning?
faq.answer: Seek medical attention if you experience: high fever (above 38.5°C / 101.5°F), blood in vomit or stool, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, signs of severe dehydration, neurological symptoms (blurred vision, muscle weakness, tingling), or if the affected person is a pregnant woman, infant, elderly adult, or immunocompromised individual.

faq.question: Can food poisoning be life-threatening?
faq.answer: Yes, in serious cases. Severe dehydration, certain bacterial infections like Listeria or E. coli O157:H7 (which can cause kidney failure), and botulism (a rare toxin that causes paralysis) can be life-threatening, especially in vulnerable populations. Prompt medical care is essential in these cases.

faq.question: What is hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)?
faq.answer: HUS is a serious complication, most often caused by E. coli O157:H7, where toxins destroy red blood cells and damage the kidneys. It is most common in young children. Symptoms include decreased urination, extreme fatigue, and pale skin after a diarrheal illness — it requires urgent hospitalization.

faq.question: Is food poisoning dangerous during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Yes. Pregnant women are at higher risk for severe food poisoning. Listeria infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery, or serious illness in the newborn. Pregnant women should avoid high-risk foods like soft cheeses, deli meats, raw seafood, and unpasteurized products.

faq.question: Are children more vulnerable to food poisoning?
faq.answer: Yes. Young children have less developed immune systems and stomach acid, making them more susceptible to foodborne illness and its complications like dehydration and HUS. Parents should ensure food is well-cooked, properly stored, and hygiene is maintained during preparation.

faq.question: Why are elderly people at greater risk from food poisoning?
faq.answer: Older adults have weakened immune systems, reduced stomach acid production, and often have underlying health conditions that make it harder to fight foodborne infections. They are more likely to develop serious complications and require hospitalization.

faq.question: How can I prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Prevent food poisoning by: washing hands thoroughly before and after handling food, cooking meat and eggs to safe internal temperatures, storing food at proper temperatures (below 5°C for cold foods), avoiding cross-contamination, not leaving cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours, and washing fruits and vegetables before eating.

faq.question: What are the safe internal cooking temperatures to prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Safe minimum internal cooking temperatures: poultry (chicken, turkey) — 74°C (165°F); ground meat — 71°C (160°F); whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb — 63°C (145°F); fish and seafood — 63°C (145°F); eggs — cook until yolk and white are firm. Use a food thermometer for accuracy.

faq.question: How long can cooked food be left out safely?
faq.answer: Cooked food should not be left at room temperature for more than 2 hours (or 1 hour if the temperature is above 32°C / 90°F). After that, bacteria multiply rapidly in the 'danger zone' between 5°C and 60°C (40°F–140°F).

faq.question: How should I store leftovers to avoid food poisoning?
faq.answer: Refrigerate leftovers in airtight containers within 2 hours of cooking. Store at or below 5°C (41°F). Consume refrigerated leftovers within 3–4 days. When reheating, ensure food reaches an internal temperature of at least 74°C (165°F) throughout.

faq.question: Does freezing food kill bacteria?
faq.answer: Freezing stops bacteria from multiplying but does not kill them. When food is thawed, bacteria can become active again. Always thaw food safely (in the refrigerator, in cold water, or in the microwave) and cook it promptly. Never refreeze thawed raw meat without cooking it first.

faq.question: How does handwashing prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Hands carry bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella from raw foods, surfaces, or the toilet. Washing hands thoroughly with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before and after handling food, after using the bathroom, and after touching animals is one of the most effective ways to prevent foodborne illness.

faq.question: What is Salmonella food poisoning?
faq.answer: Salmonella is a bacteria commonly found in raw poultry, eggs, meat, and unpasteurized dairy. Symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps beginning 6–48 hours after infection, lasting 4–7 days. Most people recover without antibiotics, but severe cases need medical treatment.

faq.question: What is E. coli food poisoning?
faq.answer: E. coli (particularly O157:H7) is found in undercooked ground beef, raw produce, and contaminated water. Symptoms include severe stomach cramps, watery or bloody diarrhea, and vomiting, starting 3–4 days after exposure. Serious cases can lead to HUS (kidney failure), especially in children.

faq.question: What is Listeria and why is it dangerous?
faq.answer: Listeria monocytogenes is a bacteria found in deli meats, soft cheeses, raw sprouts, and smoked seafood. It can grow even in the refrigerator. It is particularly dangerous for pregnant women, newborns, elderly people, and those with weakened immune systems, potentially causing meningitis, miscarriage, or death.

faq.question: What is norovirus?
faq.answer: Norovirus is the most common viral cause of food poisoning worldwide. It spreads through contaminated food, water, and surfaces, or from infected people. Symptoms — vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea — begin 12–48 hours after exposure and usually last 1–3 days. There is no specific treatment; rest and hydration are key.

faq.question: What is botulism?
faq.answer: Botulism is a rare but life-threatening illness caused by the toxin of Clostridium botulinum bacteria, commonly found in improperly canned or preserved foods. It causes weakness, blurred vision, drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing, and paralysis. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization and antitoxin treatment.

faq.question: Does reheating food always make it safe to eat?
faq.answer: Not always. Reheating kills many bacteria but does not destroy heat-stable toxins produced by bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus. Food that has been improperly stored or left out too long may still cause illness even after thorough reheating.

faq.question: Can you tell if food is contaminated by its smell or appearance?
faq.answer: No. Many dangerous bacteria (like Salmonella and E. coli) do not change the taste, smell, or appearance of food. This is why the phrase 'when in doubt, throw it out' is important — do not rely on your senses alone to judge food safety.

faq.question: Is it safe to eat food that has been in the fridge for a week?
faq.answer: Generally no. Most cooked leftovers should be consumed within 3–4 days when stored at 5°C or below. Raw meat and seafood should be cooked within 1–2 days. Even refrigerated food can harbor bacteria after too long, so label leftovers with dates and discard what is past its safe window.

faq.question: Can alcohol kill bacteria in food and prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: No. Drinking alcohol does not kill bacteria in contaminated food or protect against food poisoning. While very high concentrations of alcohol can disinfect surfaces, the alcohol consumed in drinks is far too dilute to have any antibacterial effect in the digestive system.

faq.question: Does lemon juice or vinegar make raw food safe to eat?
faq.answer: No. While acidic ingredients like lemon juice or vinegar can slow bacterial growth, they do not reliably kill all harmful pathogens in raw meat or seafood. Dishes like ceviche (raw fish marinated in citrus) still carry a risk of foodborne illness, especially for vulnerable individuals.
